weeks.title: Spiritual Authority Established by God
weeks.keyText: Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch on behalf of your souls, as those who will give account, that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be unprofitable for you.
weeks.theme: Authority comes from God and must give account to God; biblical submission is an act of faith, not blind obedience.
group: Read Hebrews 13:7, 17. What responsibilities do those who lead us have? And what responsibilities do we have?
What is your first gut reaction to the words “authority” and “submission”? What experiences lie behind that reaction?
How can we help those who lead us give their account with joy this week? Each person, name one concrete thing.
weeks.sunday: Before the service, pray for the pastor who will stand in the pulpit today and for the team leading worship, asking God to guard their hearts. As you listen to the sermon, don’t just ask, “Was it a good sermon?” Ask, “What is God asking me to obey?” If you have questions about some arrangement after the service, raise them appropriately and directly with the person responsible—rather than debating it in the parking lot.

lessons.title: Those Who Watch Over Your Soul
lessons.hear:
“Authority” and “submission” are two very unpopular words today. Some people hear them and immediately think of authoritarianism, control, and oppression; others have genuinely been hurt in church. So when we read Hebrews 13, we need to slow down and see clearly what God has said—and also what He has not said.

“Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch on behalf of your souls, as those who will give account” (Hebrews 13:17). This verse has three key points. First, God really does establish leaders in the church. From Moses asking the Lord to “appoint a man over the congregation … that the congregation of the LORD may not be as sheep which have no shepherd” (Numbers 27:16-17), to Paul saying that “the Holy Spirit has made you overseers” (Acts 20:28), God has always used people to shepherd His people. This is God’s grace, not a human invention.

Second, the essence of spiritual authority is “watching” and caring, not ruling and enjoying privileges. Leaders keep watch over your soul, like shepherds guarding a flock through the night. Third—and this is the point most often overlooked—they “will give account.” Spiritual authority is not absolute. Those who lead have a Lord above them, and they are answerable to God for how they treat the flock.

Earlier in the same chapter we read: “Remember your leaders, men who spoke to you the word of God, and considering the results of their conduct, imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13:7). What Scripture tells us to imitate is “their faith,” and we are to consider carefully the outcome of their lives. Submission is submission with our eyes open, not following with our eyes shut.

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to help you see authority afresh through God’s eyes: it is God’s way of protecting His flock, and it is also a trust for which leaders must give account to God.
lessons.light: Pride takes two forms. One is the follower who says, “Nobody can tell me what to do,” grasping the power to be his own lord. The other is the leader who says, “Everybody has to listen to me,” grasping a power that belongs only to God. Humility is returning to our proper place: leaders remember that they must give account, and followers remember that they are sheep entrusted to someone’s care. When both sides let Jesus reign, authority becomes a blessing.
think: In Hebrews 13:7, 17, how are those who lead described?
Does my response to spiritual authority lean more toward resistance or toward blind obedience?
How can I respond this week to those who lead me with “eyes-open submission”?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You that You have not left us like sheep without a shepherd, and thank You for appointing pastors to keep watch over our souls. Heal my fear of authority or my resistance to it, and keep me from blindly following people. Help me imitate the faith of those who have led me, and above all let me see that the true Head of the church is Your Son. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the name of someone who once led you and spoke the word of God to you. Think of one lesson of faith you learned from them, and send them a word of thanks. If they have already passed away, thank God for them.
lessons.quick: Spiritual authority keeps watch over my soul—and must give account to God.
text: Remember your leaders, men who spoke to you the word of God, and considering the results of their conduct, imitate their faith.

Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch on behalf of your souls, as those who will give account, that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be unprofitable for you.

lessons.title: A Humble Heart and Discerning Eyes
lessons.hear:
When she was young, one sister belonged to a church where the leader required everyone to ask his permission for everything—even making friends or changing jobs needed his nod. Anyone who raised a question was labeled “rebellious” or accused of “not submitting to God’s servant.” She eventually left, but from then on she kept every church leader at arm’s length: “I submit only to God, not to people.” Years later, at a new church, she met a pastor who was willing to listen and who could admit his own mistakes. Slowly she came to understand: her wounds were real, but the answer was not to have no shepherd at all—it was to recognize a true shepherd.

We often carry one of two old mindsets. One says, “Whatever the pastor says is what God says.” The other says, “Between me and God, I don’t need anybody.” The first is easily abused; the second easily leads to isolation.

Paul told the Ephesian elders: “Take heed, therefore, to yourselves, and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord” (Acts 20:28). Authority is appointed by the Holy Spirit—that is true. But Paul immediately warns: “Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them” (Acts 20:30). The same passage both affirms spiritual authority and warns that authority can be twisted. So biblical submission needs both a humble heart and discerning eyes.

How do we discern? Look at whom a leader is drawing people toward. A true shepherd draws people to Christ and makes them love God’s Word more; twisted authority binds people to itself, so that they grow more and more afraid of the leader and unable to leave. A true shepherd can be questioned and reminded; twisted authority labels every question as rebellion. Paul himself said, “We don’t control your faith, but are fellow workers with you for your joy” (2 Corinthians 1:24).

If you have been hurt by authority in a church, please hear this: that was not God’s heart, and you don’t have to pretend you are fine. If you carry no such wound, please be gentle with members of the body who are wary of authority; their wariness usually has a reason.
lessons.light: Blind obedience looks humble, but it may actually hand God’s place over to a person. Resistance looks spiritual, but it may actually be me wanting to reign. Both leave our proper place. To let Jesus reign is to let His Word be the measuring rod for every authority—the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide, and Jesus is my example.
think: In Acts 20:28-31, how does Paul both affirm spiritual authority and warn about it?
Is my heart closer to “Whatever the pastor says is what God says” or to “I don’t need anybody”?
Is there someone around me who has been hurt by authority and needs me to treat them gently?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You are the Good Shepherd, and You never lord it over my faith. Give me a humble heart that is willing to be shepherded, and discerning eyes that recognize Your voice. If I have shut my heart because of past hurts, heal me; if I have blindly followed people, bring me back to You. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Take ten minutes to reflect: in your church or small group, do the leaders draw people toward Christ, or bind people to themselves? Thank God for what is good. If you have concerns, write them down and seek counsel from someone you trust.
lessons.quick: Biblical submission needs a humble heart and discerning eyes.
text: Take heed, therefore, to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the assembly of the Lord and God which he purchased with his own blood.
For I know that after my departure, vicious wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock.
Men will arise from among your own selves, speaking perverse things, to draw away the disciples after them.
Therefore watch, remembering that for a period of three years I didn’t cease to admonish everyone night and day with tears.

lessons.title: A Man Under Authority
lessons.hear:
A Roman centurion once said something that made even Jesus marvel: “For I am also a man under authority, having under myself soldiers” (Matthew 8:9). He understood authority because he himself lived under authority first. He knew that his orders carried weight not because of how strong he was, but because a greater authority stood behind him. He believed that one word from Jesus would be enough, because he saw that behind Jesus’ words stood the authority of the Father.

This is the deepest secret of spiritual authority: true authority comes from submission. Jesus said, “I can of myself do nothing … because I don’t seek my own will, but the will of my Father who sent me” (John 5:30). If even the Son of God lived under the Father’s authority, then no one in the church is exempt from being under authority. Pastors are under Christ’s authority, small group leaders are under the church’s care, and every one of us is learning submission in our relationships with one another.

Today’s practice is very concrete. In your church or small group, find one arrangement that the leaders have already decided and that you have been a bit reluctant about—perhaps a change in meeting time, a serving rotation, or a new sign-up process. As long as it doesn’t contradict Scripture or harm anyone, cooperate gladly and willingly—no dragging your feet, no complaining. If you see things differently, raise it appropriately and directly with the person responsible, and then leave the outcome with God.

This kind of submission is not because the leaders are always right, but because you believe God is in control. You will find that when you stop fighting for control over every little thing, your heart actually gains freedom. Hebrews says to let leaders do their work “with joy, and not with groaning” (Hebrews 13:17), because their groaning would ultimately be of no benefit to you either.
lessons.light: Pride grasps power; humility lays it down. Gladly cooperating in small things is a way of laying it down: I don’t have to be in charge of everything. The focus is on Jesus, not on who is right or wrong. When I trust that He reigns, I can rest securely under human authority—and I can also speak honest opinions with a quiet heart. This is the freedom of the selfless life.
think: In Matthew 8:5-10, how does the centurion understand authority?
In what small matter have I been reluctant to cooperate with those who lead?
How will I cooperate willingly today, or express my opinion in an appropriate way?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You gladly lived under the Father’s authority, seeking only His will in everything. Take away my need to be in charge of everything. Help me cooperate willingly with arrangements that are in line with the truth, and when I disagree, help me speak the truth in love. Teach me in small things to trust that You reign. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose one arrangement in your church or small group that you were reluctant about but that is in line with Scripture, and cooperate with it gladly. Then send a short word of thanks or encouragement to the ministry team member responsible for it.
lessons.quick: True authority comes from submission; gladness in small things is trust that God reigns.
text: When he came into Capernaum, a centurion came to him, asking him for help,
saying, “Lord, my servant lies in the house paralyzed, grievously tormented.”
Jesus said to him, “I will come and heal him.”
The centurion answered, “Lord, I’m not worthy for you to come under my roof. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed.
For I am also a man under authority, having under myself soldiers. I tell this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and tell another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and tell my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”
When Jesus heard it, he marveled and said to those who followed, “Most certainly I tell you, I haven’t found so great a faith, not even in Israel.

lessons.title: David’s Cave and Nathan’s Words
lessons.hear:
“Don’t touch the Lord’s anointed” is quoted often in Chinese churches—and misused often. Let’s go back to the original scene. Saul was hunting David down, and David was hiding in a cave. Saul happened to come into that very cave, and David’s men said this was his chance. David only cut off the edge of Saul’s robe, yet afterward “David’s heart struck him” (1 Samuel 24:5), and he said, “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him” (1 Samuel 24:6).

This passage teaches us not to take revenge with our own hands and not to seize a position God has not given us. David left judgment to God, and that was profound humility. But notice two other things as well. First, David did not stay at Saul’s side and let himself be speared. When Saul hurled his spear, “David fled, and escaped that night” (1 Samuel 19:10). Respecting an office God has established does not mean staying in danger and letting someone harm you. Second, David told the truth to Saul’s face: “Why do you listen to men’s words?” (1 Samuel 24:9). Later, when David himself was king and committed a great sin, God sent the prophet Nathan to confront him directly: “You are the man” (2 Samuel 12:7). In God’s kingdom, even the highest authority must be brought into the light of truth.

So today’s review has two sides. On one side: have I been gossiping behind leaders’ backs, making snide remarks, or quietly forming factions—turning my dissatisfaction into little “robe-cutting” moves? If so, I need to repent and learn to speak directly and appropriately. On the other side: if you or someone near you is experiencing spiritual abuse, sexual harassment, violence, or financial misconduct, please know clearly that this is not a lesson in “submission.” You can, and should, seek help from a trusted third party, the church’s denominational or oversight body, a professional counselor, or even legal channels. Those who are harmed do not have to keep silent for the sake of “unity”; Scripture itself commands us to “relieve the oppressed” (Isaiah 1:17).

True unity is built on truth and righteousness, not on cover-ups.
lessons.light: Self-centered rebellion is me wanting to reign, seizing power through gossip and factions. Self-centered silence is fearing people more than God, covering sin with the word “unity.” The selfless person returns to their proper place: not seizing God’s right to judge, and not laying down the justice God has entrusted to us. To let Jesus reign is to let His truth rule in the light.
think: In 1 Samuel 24, how did David honor Saul without letting Saul harm him?
Has my dissatisfaction with leaders turned into “robe-cutting” behind their backs?
If someone needs protection, do I know where they can turn for help?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, forgive me for talking behind the backs of those who lead and for expressing my dissatisfaction through small, petty moves. Give me courage, when it is needed, to speak up for the oppressed, and never to cover harm in the name of unity. You are a God of justice and a God of love; may Your truth reign in Your church. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If you have talked about a leader behind their back, confess it to God today and consider sharing your perspective with that person directly and gently. If you know someone who has suffered abuse of power or harm, go with them to find a trusted person or professional help.
lessons.quick: Honoring an office never means covering up harm; true unity is built on truth.
text: David’s men said to him, “Behold, the day of which the LORD said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you.’” Then David arose and cut off the skirt of Saul’s robe secretly.
Afterward, David’s heart struck him because he had cut off Saul’s skirt.
He said to his men, “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD’s anointed, to stretch out my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed.”
So David checked his men with these words, and didn’t allow them to rise against Saul. Saul rose up out of the cave, and went on his way.
David also arose afterward, and went out of the cave and cried after Saul, saying, “My lord the king!” When Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the earth, and showed respect.
David said to Saul, “Why do you listen to men’s words, saying, ‘Behold, David seeks to harm you’?

Behold, today your eyes have seen how the LORD had delivered you today into my hand in the cave. Some urged me to kill you, but I spared you. I said, ‘I will not stretch out my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD’s anointed.’

lessons.title: Under Authority, Able to Lead
lessons.hear:
While Israel was still in the wilderness, God set down rules for their future kings. Once a king took the throne, he was to write out his own copy of the law: “It shall be with him, and he shall read from it all the days of his life” (Deuteronomy 17:19), so “that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers” (Deuteronomy 17:20). Picture the scene: the most powerful man in the nation sitting down every day to copy and read God’s Word, reminding himself that he too is just one brother among God’s people.

This week we have seen that God establishes spiritual authority to care for His flock; that authority must give account to God; that submission needs both a humble heart and discerning eyes; that true authority comes from submission; and that honoring an office never means covering up harm. It all comes down to one sentence: every authority stands under the Word of God.

This truth is not only for pastors. It is for everyone who “leads others”: parents, small group leaders, workplace managers, children’s ministry teachers, choir directors, administrators of online groups. If anyone follows you, you hold a measure of authority. Ask yourself: Am I a person who lives under authority? Am I willing to be held accountable? Do the people who follow me become more afraid of me, or do they come to love God more? Jesus said, “But he who is greatest among you will be your servant” (Matthew 23:11).

The way to multiply is to pass this healthy view of authority on. When you teach your children, let them see you admit your wrongs before God. When you lead a small group, invite members to give you feedback. In the workplace, manage as a servant. If the next generation sees healthy authority with their own eyes, they will be far less likely to fall into either extreme of blind obedience or rebellion.
lessons.light: Those who can lead others must first be people who are led. Change begins with me: only as I live under God’s Word will I carry spiritual weight before others. Pass what you have received on to your “2”—your children, group members, and coworkers—so they can see that authority can be warm, accountable, and freeing.
think: In Deuteronomy 17:18-20, why did God want the king to copy and read the law?
In my roles of leading others, am I willing to be held accountable?
How will I let those who follow me see healthy authority this week?
lessons.speak: Lord, You are the King of kings, and I am under Your authority. Help me humble myself before Your Word every day, and never become proud before my family, group members, or coworkers. Make me a leader who welcomes accountability and helps people love You more, and let me pass healthy spiritual authority on to the next generation. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, ask one person you lead (a child, a group member, or a coworker): “When I lead you, is there anything that makes you feel pressured?” Listen quietly, without rushing to explain.
lessons.quick: Every authority stands under the Word of God—including mine.
text: It shall be, when he sits on the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write himself a copy of this law in a book, out of that which is before the Levitical priests.
It shall be with him, and he shall read from it all the days of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them;

that his heart not be lifted up above his brothers, and that he not turn away from the commandment to the right hand, or to the left, to the end that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he and his children, in the middle of Israel.

weeks.title: Pastors as Servants: The Chief Shepherd and Under-Shepherds
weeks.keyText: shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily; not for dishonest gain, but willingly;
weeks.theme: Jesus is the Chief Shepherd and pastors are servants under Him; understand their calling and bear with their weaknesses.
group: Read 1 Peter 5:1-4. What three “not … but …” contrasts does Peter set before shepherds?
What does your ideal pastor look like? Where did that picture come from?
What practical steps can we take this week so that our pastor or small group leader feels cared for as a person?
weeks.sunday: As you look at the pastor in the pulpit, remind yourself: he too is a sheep being shepherded by the Chief Shepherd. Before the service, pray for him and ask the Lord to strengthen him. As you listen, remember that the power of the message comes from God, not from the clay jar. After the service, try greeting him with something that has nothing to do with the sermon: “How are you and your family doing lately?”

lessons.title: Shepherds Under the Chief Shepherd
lessons.hear:
The man who wrote 1 Peter 5 was a man who had once denied the Lord three times. He didn’t present himself as the “chief apostle.” Instead he wrote, “I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder, and a witness of the sufferings of Christ” (1 Peter 5:1). He placed himself among his co-workers, not high above them.

Then he states the core calling of a shepherd: “shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight” (1 Peter 5:2). Notice the words “the flock of God.” The sheep do not belong to the shepherd; they belong to God. A pastor is not the owner of the flock but a steward entrusted with it. Peter then gives three contrasts in a row: “not under compulsion, but voluntarily, not for dishonest gain, but willingly; not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2-3). These three contrasts aim precisely at the three places where pastors most easily stumble: weariness, money, and power.

Finally, Peter lifts our eyes to the future: “When the chief Shepherd is revealed” (1 Peter 5:4). The church has only one Chief Shepherd—Jesus, who said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Every pastor is an under-shepherd serving beneath this great Shepherd. Their authority is entrusted to them, and their crown will be given by the Lord in the future.

Understanding this changes both the way we see pastors and the way pastors see themselves. We no longer put pastors on a pedestal, nor do we treat them as hired staff. And pastors don’t have to play the all-powerful hero, because the true Shepherd of the flock is the Lord Jesus. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to help you see the one who stands before you: a servant entrusted by the Lord, and also a sheep who, like you, looks to the Chief Shepherd.
lessons.light: The words “the flock of God” return pastors to their proper place: the sheep are not mine; they are God’s. Self-centered shepherding treats the sheep as personal achievements; selfless shepherding hands the sheep back to the Lord. The same goes for church members—I belong to Christ, not to any pastor. So I can respect my pastor without worshiping him.
think: In 1 Peter 5:1-4, what does Peter call himself? And what does he call Jesus?
Do I see a particular pastor as too high—or too low?
How can I see my pastor this week as “a servant under the Lord”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You are the Good Shepherd and the Chief Shepherd. Thank You for laying down Your life for me, and thank You for sending pastors to care for Your flock. Keep them serving voluntarily, willingly, and as examples to the flock. Help me neither to idolize people nor to look down on Your servants, but to look to You alone. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, using the three contrasts in 1 Peter 5:2-3, pray one sentence for each of your church’s pastors: ask the Lord to keep them serving voluntarily, willingly, and as examples to the flock.
lessons.quick: The sheep are God’s, pastors are servants, and the church has only one Chief Shepherd.
text: Therefore I exhort the elders among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and who will also share in the glory that will be revealed:
shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily; not for dishonest gain, but willingly;
not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.
When the chief Shepherd is revealed, you will receive the crown of glory that doesn’t fade away.

lessons.title: Whoever Would Be First Must Serve
lessons.hear:
When one church was hiring a new pastor, the members drew up a long list of expectations: his preaching had to be brilliant, he had to know management, lead worship, attract young people, and answer the phone twenty-four hours a day—and ideally his wife would serve full-time too. Someone said, “We pay his salary, so he should deliver.” Another church was the exact opposite: everyone treated the pastor like a celebrity. Whatever he said was right, and his photo was more prominent than the cross. The two churches looked different, but they made the same mistake: they saw their pastor through the world’s eyes—one as an employee, the other as a boss.

The disciples once thought the same way. James and John asked Jesus to let them sit at His right and left in His glory. When the other disciples found out, they were indignant, because they wanted those seats too. Jesus called them together and said, “You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you” (Mark 10:42-43).

“It shall not be so among you”—with these words Jesus drew a boundary line for His kingdom. Leadership in the world climbs upward; leadership in God’s kingdom bends down. “Whoever of you wants to become first among you, shall be bondservant of all. For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve” (Mark 10:44-45). Paul described himself the same way: “For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake” (2 Corinthians 4:5).

Notice the words “for Jesus’ sake.” A pastor is a servant, but first of all he is Christ’s servant, not the congregation’s employee. He serves you because the Lord sent him, not because you pay him; he leads you because the Lord entrusted him with it, not because he ranks above you. When we see pastors this way, we won’t treat them as staff to be ordered around, nor will we lift them onto a throne that belongs to God alone.
lessons.light: Pride climbs upward and grasps power; humility bends down and returns to its proper place. When a pastor serves with a servant’s heart, he is imitating Jesus—Jesus is my example. When members treat a pastor as an employee, they want to be in charge themselves; when they treat a pastor as an idol, they give God’s place to a person. Both need to return to God’s perspective.
think: In Mark 10:42-45, how does Jesus contrast leadership in the world with leadership in God’s kingdom?
Are my expectations of my pastor more like expectations of an employee or of a celebrity?
How will I adjust my expectations of my pastor so that they line up with God’s perspective?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You are Lord of lords, yet You bent down to serve me and gave Your life for me. Forgive me for looking at Your servants through the world’s eyes—sometimes making harsh demands, sometimes putting them on a pedestal. Help me see my pastor through Your eyes, and teach me to become a servant of all. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down three expectations you have of your pastor. For each one, ask: “Is this a biblical requirement, or just my own preference?” Hand any inappropriate expectations over to the Lord, and pray once for your pastor.
lessons.quick: A pastor is Christ’s servant—not the congregation’s employee, and not the church’s celebrity.
text: Jesus summoned them and said to them, “You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first among you shall be bondservant of all.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.title: Treasure in Clay Jars
lessons.hear:
Paul says, “But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 4:7). In the ancient world, clay jars were the most ordinary household items—easily cracked, easily broken, cheap, and unremarkable. Yet it was in vessels like these that God chose to place the priceless treasure of the gospel. Pastors are exactly such clay jars.

We often forget that pastors are human. They get tired, they get anxious, they say the wrong thing, and their families have struggles they can’t talk about. Paul frankly admitted, “There is that which presses on me daily: anxiety for all the assemblies” (2 Corinthians 11:28). When the people of Lystra tried to offer sacrifices to Paul and Barnabas, the two tore their clothes and cried out, “We also are men of the same nature as you” (Acts 14:15). One pastor said that his loneliest moment was standing on the platform on Sunday, looking out at hundreds of faces, and not knowing whether anyone would ask him on Monday, “Are you doing okay?”

Today’s practice is to love your pastor as a person:
1. Ask about him, not just about church matters—Have you been sleeping well lately? How are your kids?
2. Give him a specific word of thanks—not just “Great sermon,” but “That message last month helped me get through a hard season.”
3. Take on one small task—volunteer for a piece of ministry you are able to do, so he has one less thing weighing on him.

Bearing with a pastor’s weaknesses is not making excuses for his sin; it is acknowledging that he needs grace just as much as we do. When we treat clay jars with grace, they are better able to hold the treasure—and God’s power is made perfect in human weakness.
lessons.light: People matter more than programs. We often see only a pastor’s “ministry” and forget his “life.” Life first, then relationships, then ministry: caring for the pastor as a person comes before evaluating his performance. Through the lens of 920, my pastor is also one of my “2,” and in my relationship with him I can bear the fruit of kindness and goodness.
think: In 2 Corinthians 4:5-7, how does Paul see himself, and how does he see the gospel he preaches?
When was the last time I cared for my pastor as a “person” rather than as a “position”?
Which of these three things can I choose to do today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You for putting treasure in clay jars, and thank You for using weak people to shepherd me. Help me treat my pastor with grace and see him as a person who needs to be loved and supported. When he is weary, comfort him Yourself, and let Your power be made perfect in his weakness. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to your pastor or small group leader that simply asks how they and their family are doing, without mentioning any church business—or write a specific word of thanks and give it to them.
lessons.quick: Pastors are clay jars—and they need to be loved as people.
text: For we don’t preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake,
seeing it is God who said, “Light will shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God and not from ourselves.

lessons.title: Shepherds Who Feed Only Themselves
lessons.hear:
Ezekiel 34 is a stern mirror. Through the prophet, God rebukes the leaders of Israel: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep?” (Ezekiel 34:2). They ate the fat and wore the wool, but they did not care for the weak, the sick, or the injured; instead, “you have ruled over them with force and with rigor” (Ezekiel 34:4). As a result, the flock was scattered and became food for wild animals.

This passage speaks first to everyone who leads. You may be a pastor, or a small group leader, fellowship officer, children’s ministry teacher, or administrator of an online group. Ask yourself honestly: Do I serve in order to be seen and needed, or for the good of the flock? Do I care about attendance numbers, or about the person who hasn’t shown up for three weeks? Can I receive correction from others? “Feeding only themselves” often doesn’t begin with greed for money; it begins with a craving for affirmation and a fear of losing influence.

This passage is also God’s promise to wounded sheep. God does not say, “You must put up with bad shepherds.” He says, “Behold, I am against the shepherds … I will deliver my sheep from their mouth” (Ezekiel 34:10), and again, “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep” (Ezekiel 34:15). God stands on the side of the wounded sheep. So if you encounter spiritual abuse, sexual harassment, violence, or financial misconduct in a church, please don’t stay silent or blame yourself just because the person is a “pastor.” Seeking help from trusted elders and deacons, the church’s denominational or oversight body, a professional counselor, or the appropriate authorities is exactly how God’s justice is displayed in His house.

Correction and restoration are always possible. Peter once fell, and the Lord restored him by the Sea of Galilee; a shepherd who is willing to repent and accept accountability can still be used by God. But restoration must happen in the truth, never in a cover-up.
lessons.light: “Feeding only themselves” is self-centered shepherding—centered on oneself, treating the flock as one’s own resource. The selfless shepherd remembers that the sheep are God’s and that he is only a servant entrusted with them. Being willing to be held accountable and to admit mistakes is a mark of humility; refusing all correction is a warning sign of pride. To let Jesus reign is to let His heart rank above my influence.
think: In Ezekiel 34:2-10, what failures of the shepherds does God point out? What will God Himself do?
Where I lead or influence others, are there any signs of “feeding only myself”?
If someone has been hurt in the church, do I know how to walk with them as they seek help?
lessons.speak: Jesus, great Shepherd, search the motives of my service. If in any position of leadership I have been looking out only for myself, shine Your light on me and lead me to repentance. Protect the sheep who have been wounded in the church, bind up their wounds Yourself, and give Your church courage to face the truth and be cleansed in justice and mercy. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If you lead others in any role, ask a co-worker you trust today: “Is there anything in my ministry you think I need to adjust?” Listen quietly and write down one adjustment you will make.
lessons.quick: The sheep are God’s; He stands with the wounded sheep and restores the repentant shepherd.
text: “Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel. Prophesy, and tell them, even the shepherds, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves! Shouldn’t the shepherds feed the sheep?
You eat the fat. You clothe yourself with the wool. You kill the fatlings, but you don’t feed the sheep.

You haven’t strengthened the diseased. You haven’t healed that which was sick. You haven’t bound up that which was broken. You haven’t brought back that which was driven away. You haven’t sought that which was lost, but you have ruled over them with force and with rigor.
They were scattered, because there was no shepherd. They became food to all the animals of the field, and were scattered.
My sheep wandered through all the mountains and on every high hill. Yes, my sheep were scattered on all the surface of the earth. There was no one who searched or sought.”
“‘Therefore, you shepherds, hear the LORD’s word:

“As I live,” says the Lord GOD, “surely because my sheep became a prey, and my sheep became food to all the animals of the field, because there was no shepherd, and my shepherds didn’t search for my sheep, but the shepherds fed themselves, and didn’t feed my sheep,
therefore, you shepherds, hear the LORD’s word!”

The Lord GOD says: “Behold, I am against the shepherds. I will require my sheep at their hand, and cause them to cease from feeding the sheep. The shepherds won’t feed themselves any more. I will deliver my sheep from their mouth, that they may not be food for them.”

lessons.title: Feed My Lambs
lessons.hear:
It is morning on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, and the charcoal fire is still burning. Not long before, it was beside a charcoal fire that Peter denied the Lord three times. Now the risen Lord asks him three times, “Do you love me?” Each time Peter answers, Jesus gives him a charge: “Feed my lambs” (John 21:15). “Tend my sheep” (John 21:16).

This scene ties together the theme of the whole week. First, the qualification for shepherding is not perfection but love for the Lord. Peter was not called because he had never failed, but because he had been restored by the Lord and loved Him. Second, the sheep are always “my sheep”—they belong to the Lord, not to Peter. Third, years later Peter wrote to the elders urging them to “shepherd the flock of God which is among you,” passing on the charge he had received to the next generation of shepherds.

This calling does not belong only to full-time pastors. In certain relationships, every Christian can become an under-shepherd: parents shepherd their children, group members look after newcomers, mature brothers and sisters walk alongside new believers, and in the Air Fellowship someone sends a private message every week to check in on a member far away. There is only one Chief Shepherd, but there can be tens of thousands of under-shepherds. In Ezekiel God promises, “I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken” (Ezekiel 34:16)—and today He often does these things through ordinary pairs of hands.

This week, please pass on two things. The first is a right view of pastors: they are the Lord’s servants and also people who need to be loved. The second is the calling of an under-shepherd: invite a brother or sister to join you in caring for one lamb the Lord has entrusted to you.
lessons.light: The spiritual parents and children (3) of 235 are the passing on of the under-shepherd’s life. The Way of Service begins with “Spirit” and ends with “God”: led by the Holy Spirit to love one person, and in the end giving the glory to the Chief Shepherd. The focus is not on how many people I have shepherded, but on whether Jesus reigns in their hearts.
think: In John 21:15-17, what did Jesus entrust to Peter three times?
How has my view of pastors and of “under-shepherds” changed this week?
Who is the “lamb” the Lord wants me to begin walking alongside?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You asked Peter, “Do you love me?”—and today You ask me the same. Lord, You know that I love You, even though I am often weak. Make me an under-shepherd serving under You—at home, in my small group, at work, or online—feeding the lambs You entrust to me, and giving all the glory to You, the Chief Shepherd. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose one newcomer, new believer, or less-often-seen group member you can walk alongside. Arrange to meet or talk with them once this week, and pray for them regularly every week.
lessons.quick: There is only one Chief Shepherd, but there can be countless under-shepherds.
text: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

weeks.title: Praying For, Supporting, and Honoring Pastors
weeks.keyText: But we beg you, brothers, to know those who labor among you, and are over you in the Lord and admonish you,
weeks.theme: Hold up Moses’ hands: through prayer, honor, and practical action, stand with our pastors on the hilltop.
group: Read 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13. How does Paul urge us to treat those who lead us, and why?
Have you ever criticized a pastor or ministry team member behind their back? What was going on in your heart at the time?
What one concrete act of support can our small group offer our pastor or small group leader this week? Who will take responsibility for it?
weeks.sunday: Before the service, like Aaron and Hur, lift up in prayer those who will preach and lead today. During the sermon, if a sentence helps you, write it down. After the service, tell the pastor—in person or on a small card—how that sentence helped you. One specific word of thanks is often a pastor’s strength for the whole week.

lessons.title: For Their Work’s Sake
lessons.hear:
The church in Thessalonica was very young. Paul had stayed there only a short time before he was forced to leave, and most of the leaders left behind were beginners themselves. At the end of his letter, Paul gives a special charge: “But we beg you, brothers, to know those who labor among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you, and to respect and honor them in love for their work’s sake” (1 Thessalonians 5:12-13).

Three phrases in this passage are worth savoring. The first is “labor.” The first word Paul uses for leaders is not “gifted” or “prominent,” but “those who labor.” Shepherding is exhausting work: late-night phone calls, hospital corridors, funeral pulpits, arguments in team meetings. The second is “in the Lord.” Their leading and admonishing take place in the Lord; to honor them is ultimately to honor the Lord who sent them. The third is “for their work’s sake.” The basis for honor is not titles, degrees, or eloquence, but the labor they have poured out for the Lord and for you.

Paul then adds: “Be at peace among yourselves” (1 Thessalonians 5:13). That is no coincidence. Much of the conflict in churches begins with dissatisfaction toward leaders quietly fermenting behind the scenes; healthy honor for leaders is often the foundation of peace for the whole church.

Biblical honor is not a personality cult, and it doesn’t mean you can never voice an opinion. It is an attitude of seeing with love and responding with gratitude. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes to those who labor around you: perhaps your senior pastor, perhaps a small group leader who has served quietly for years, or a ministry team member still editing recordings for the Air Fellowship late at night. God remembers all their labor; may the Lord teach us to remember it too.
lessons.light: The order of relationships is God first, then people. Honoring those who lead is an extension of fearing God, because they labor “in the Lord.” The self-centered person sees a pastor’s shortcomings first; the selfless person sees their labor first. Grateful eyes turn us from critics into supporters, and let Jesus receive the glory.
think: In 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13, what words does Paul use to describe those who lead?
Who are the people laboring around me whom I have never really noticed?
How can I “respect and honor them in love” this week—at least one of them?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You for placing so many people around me who labor for my sake. Forgive me for so often seeing only their shortcomings and forgetting what they have given. Give me grateful eyes to honor them in love, and make our church a place where we are at peace with one another, so that Jesus receives the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, list three people in your church who labor for you (a pastor, a small group leader, or a behind-the-scenes ministry team member). Next to each name, write one specific thing you are thankful to them for.
lessons.quick: Honor is not worship; it is seeing their labor in the Lord.
text: But we beg you, brothers, to know those who labor among you, and are over you in the Lord and admonish you,
and to respect and honor them in love for their work’s sake. Be at peace among yourselves.

lessons.title: Double Honor, Fair Accountability
lessons.hear:
One pastor served a small church for fifteen years. The church was not well off financially, and he never asked for a raise; his wife worked part-time outside to help cover the household budget. Later, when he was hospitalized with an illness, a member posted in the group chat: “Ministers are supposed to sacrifice anyway.” In that same group chat, a baseless rumor had once circulated claiming that the pastor was misusing the offerings. It was forwarded again and again, yet no one ever checked whether it was true.

Behind both incidents lies the same old mindset: a pastor’s needs don’t matter, and neither does a pastor’s reputation. Paul sees it completely differently: “Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and in teaching” (1 Timothy 5:17). “Double honor” includes respect, and it also includes practical provision, because Paul goes on to quote the law: “You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain” (1 Timothy 5:18). Caring for a pastor’s livelihood is not charity; it is justice.

Paul also protects a pastor’s reputation: “Don’t receive an accusation against an elder, except at the word of two or three witnesses” (1 Timothy 5:19). This does not mean pastors can never be accused; it means no one may be condemned on the basis of rumor. The next verse makes it even clearer: “Those who sin, reprove in the sight of all” (1 Timothy 5:20). Scripture does two things at once: it protects pastors from being wounded by gossip, and it ensures that when pastors truly do wrong, they are held fairly accountable.

This is biblical honor—neither mistreating nor shielding. We provide for our pastors in love and don’t let rumors run loose in the group chat. At the same time, if there really is misconduct, we handle it through proper process and with real evidence, bringing it to the elders and deacons board or the church’s denominational or oversight body, and seeking professional help when needed. Honor and accountability are not opposites: precisely because we value this office, we will not let it be stained by sin, nor let it be destroyed by rumor.
lessons.light: Mistreating a pastor and shielding a pastor are both self-centered: one wants to be in control, the other is afraid of offending people. The selfless person returns to their proper place and sees pastors from God’s perspective: worthy of double honor, and also required to be accountable in the truth. The Bible is my standard—not the emotions in a group chat. The Holy Spirit is my guide—not whatever everyone else is saying.
think: In 1 Timothy 5:17-20, how does Paul both protect pastors and require accountability?
Have I ever forwarded or believed unverified claims about a pastor?
How can I treat my pastor more biblically in both provision and accountability?
lessons.speak: Lord, forgive me for the times I have made light of my pastor’s needs, and for the times I have easily believed or passed along unverified words. Help me provide for Your servants in love and guard Your house with truth—courageous when accountability is needed, and restrained when facing rumors. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, if you hear a negative rumor about a pastor or ministry team member, decide not to pass it on. If you have a genuine concern, write it down and ask a suitable, trustworthy elder or deacon about it directly.
lessons.quick: Double honor and fair accountability—neither mistreating nor shielding.
text: Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and in teaching.
For the Scripture says, “You shall not muzzle the ox when it treads out the grain.” And, “The laborer is worthy of his wages.”
Don’t receive an accusation against an elder except at the word of two or three witnesses.
Those who sin, reprove in the sight of all, that the rest also may be in fear.

lessons.title: Holding Up Moses’ Hands
lessons.hear:
At Rephidim, Israel went to war with the Amalekites. Joshua fought in the valley while Moses stood on the hilltop with his hands raised. Here is the remarkable part: “When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed. When he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed” (Exodus 17:11). But Moses was only human, and his hands grew heavy. So Aaron and Hur brought a stone for him to sit on, and “Aaron and Hur held up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side. His hands were steady until sunset” (Exodus 17:12).

This is the most beautiful picture in Scripture of supporting a leader. The victory did not belong to Moses alone; it was won by three people on the hilltop together with the whole army in the valley. Hur’s name rarely appears in the Bible. He didn’t preach, and he didn’t command troops; he simply held up one hand. But without him, that day’s battle might have been lost.

Paul often asked the churches for prayer: “Brothers, pray for us” (1 Thessalonians 5:25). His requests were usually very specific—asking God to open a door for the word, so that he could proclaim the gospel boldly. Today’s practice is to become a Hur for one of your pastors:
1. Pray specifically—not just “Bless the pastor,” but pray separately for his health, his family, his preaching, his decisions, and his spiritual life;
2. Support specifically—take on one task yourself, or help shield him from one unnecessary distraction;
3. Encourage specifically—let him know that someone is standing with him on the hilltop.

Those who hold up hands don’t need to be seen. Perhaps your prayer is the very stone that keeps a weary pastor from letting his hands drop this week.
lessons.light: The final step of the Way of Service is “God”: letting Jesus receive all the glory. Hur did not seek to be seen—that is selfless service. We pray for our pastors not so that they will remember us, but so that God’s kingdom will prevail in the battle. People matter more than tasks—holding up one person’s hands is often more important than finishing one more job.
think: In Exodus 17:8-13, how was the victory won? What did Aaron and Hur do?
Do I more often pray for my pastor, or comment on my pastor?
For which area of my pastor’s life will I pray specifically this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank You for giving me a pastor. Today I want to be his Hur and hold up his heavy hands. Strengthen his body, guard his family, anoint his lips when he preaches, give him wisdom when he makes decisions, and comfort him Yourself when he is weary. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, spend five minutes praying specifically for your pastor’s health, family, preaching, decisions, and spiritual life. Then send him a message: “I prayed for you today. Is there anything in particular you’d like me to pray for?”
lessons.quick: Be a Hur—hold up your pastor’s heavy hands.
text: Then Amalek came and fought with Israel in Rephidim.
Moses said to Joshua, “Choose men for us, and go out to fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with God’s rod in my hand.”
So Joshua did as Moses had told him, and fought with Amalek; and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed. When he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.

But Moses’ hands were heavy; so they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur held up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side. His hands were steady until sunset.
Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.

lessons.title: The God Who Comforts the Lowly
lessons.hear:
Many people imagine Paul as an apostle made of steel, but he frankly admits: “our flesh had no relief, but we were afflicted on every side. Fightings were outside. Fear was inside” (2 Corinthians 7:5). And one of the things troubling his heart was the Corinthian church itself. This church had criticized his appearance and his speaking, questioned his motives, and compared him with other preachers; some among them had caused him deep sorrow. Paul had written to them “with many tears,” and his heart could not let them go.

Then came the turning point: “Nevertheless, he who comforts the lowly, God, comforted us by the coming of Titus” (2 Corinthians 7:6). The news Titus brought was this: the Corinthians had repented. They longed for Paul, mourned over what had happened, and had a renewed zeal for him. A church that had once broken its pastor’s heart became a church that comforted its pastor.

This is the hope behind today’s review and adjustment. Look back honestly: Have I, like the Corinthians, been comparing, nitpicking, or cold toward my pastor or ministry team members? Do I only show up when I’m unhappy, and never when I’m grateful? Do I treat my pastor as a service provider—use and move on? Pastors are people who can be brought low too; sometimes a single cold remark keeps one awake all night.

Adjustment can begin with a simple turning around. If you have criticized him unfairly, you can apologize privately. If you have always been silent, you can speak a word of thanks. And to be clear: this adjustment targets unfair criticism and indifference; it does not ask you to take back genuine concerns. Reminders grounded in truth can and should still be spoken in love.

Paul says this news meant “that I rejoiced still more” (2 Corinthians 7:7). Today, you too might be the person God uses to comfort a pastor.
lessons.light: Pride provokes pride: members nitpick, the pastor gets defensive, and everyone loses. Humility inspires humility: one sincere apology or word of thanks often makes a pastor more willing to listen. Change begins with me—I don’t have to wait for the pastor to change first. I can return to my proper place first, become a vessel of God’s comfort, and let humility spread humility throughout the church.
think: In 2 Corinthians 7:5-7, what was Paul going through? How did God comfort him?
In my attitude toward my pastor, what resembles the Corinthians’ comparing and nitpicking?
To whom do I need to apologize, or offer an overdue word of thanks?
lessons.speak: God who comforts the lowly, I confess that I have treated Your servants with comparison, nitpicking, or coldness, making their burdens heavier. Forgive me, and give me courage to change. Let me be a Titus whom You use to comfort my pastors, bringing them joy rather than sorrow. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If you have unfairly criticized a pastor or ministry team member, send them a private apology today. If not, write a specific thank-you card or message to let them know what their ministry means to you.
lessons.quick: A church that once broke its pastor’s heart can become a church that comforts its pastor.
text: For even when we had come into Macedonia, our flesh had no relief, but we were afflicted on every side. Fightings were outside. Fear was inside.
Nevertheless, he who comforts the lowly, God, comforted us by the coming of Titus,
and not by his coming only, but also by the comfort with which he was comforted in you while he told us of your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.

lessons.title: Partners in Affliction
lessons.hear:
There was a beautiful partnership between the Philippian church and Paul. Paul writes, “No assembly shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving but you only” (Philippians 4:15). They provided for Paul more than once, and even sent Epaphroditus to care for him in person. Paul describes their gift as “a sweet-smelling fragrance, an acceptable and well-pleasing sacrifice to God” (Philippians 4:18).

Notice Paul’s heart: “Not that I seek for the gift, but I seek for the fruit that increases to your account” (Philippians 4:17). When we support our pastors, the ones who benefit in the end are not only the pastors but also those who give the support. When you pray for your pastor, honor him, and provide for him, you are storing up eternal fruit in God’s kingdom. Paul also gives such a church a promise: “My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19).

This week we began by honoring those who labor among us. We learned about double honor and fair accountability, learned to be a Hur who holds up tired hands, and learned to be a Titus who brings comfort to a pastor. Now it is time to turn what we have received into a culture and pass it on. Supporting pastors should not be just the private initiative of a few enthusiastic people; it should become a habit of the whole small group and the whole church: small group members taking turns to pray for the pastor, someone keeping an eye on the needs of the pastor’s family, someone stepping into ministry roles when the pastor is on leave so that he can truly rest.

In the Air Fellowship, pastors and ministry team members often serve across time zones. Perhaps you could start a small “Hold Up the Hands” initiative, inviting your group members to pray each week for one ministry team member and send them a word of encouragement. When the next generation sees how we love our pastors, they will know how to love the church in the years to come.
lessons.light: Multiplication is not only passing on truth; it is also passing on culture. The Philippian church made support a habit of the whole church and became Paul’s partners in affliction. The comrades-in-arms (5) of 235 are exactly this—supporting one another and fighting side by side. Let Jesus receive all the glory, and let none of His servants stand alone.
think: In Philippians 4:14-19, how did the Philippian church support Paul? How did Paul view their support?
What concrete change has there been in my attitude toward my pastor this week?
Whom can I invite to join me in starting an initiative to support our pastors?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You for helping me see my pastors’ labor afresh this week. Make our small group and our church like the Philippian church—sharing in our pastors’ afflictions and their victories. May our support be a fragrance that pleases You, and an example from which the next generation learns to love the church. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, invite one or two group members to start a “Hold Up the Hands” initiative for a pastor or ministry team member: each of you prays for them once this week, and on the weekend you send them a word of encouragement or a small gift together.
lessons.quick: Supporting pastors is not just a personal act; it is the culture of the whole church.
text: However you did well that you shared in my affliction.
You yourselves also know, you Philippians, that in the beginning of the Good News, when I departed from Macedonia, no assembly shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving but you only.
For even in Thessalonica you sent once and again to my need.
Not that I seek for the gift, but I seek for the fruit that increases to your account.
But I have all things and abound. I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things that came from you, a sweet-smelling fragrance, an acceptable and well-pleasing sacrifice to God.
My God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

weeks.title: When We Disagree
weeks.keyText: but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,
weeks.theme: When we disagree, we neither go silent nor form factions; we speak the truth in love and grow up together into Christ, the head.
group: Read Ephesians 4:15 and Matthew 18:15. Which is harder for you: “speaking truth” or going to someone “between you and him alone”?
When have you seen a disagreement handled well (or badly)? What did you learn from it?
This week we agree not to talk about others behind their backs. When someone starts to, what is one gentle sentence we could use to stop it?
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, if you disagree with something at church, hand it to the Lord before the service begins: “Lord, I will let you reign, not my emotions.” During the service, focus on worship instead of keeping score in your head. Afterward, if you need to say something, say it privately and gently to the person responsible—not in the hallway.

lessons.title: Speaking Truth in Love
lessons.hear:
In church, disagreement is only a matter of time. New songs or old hymns? Should the budget go to a building or to missions? Should the small group multiply? Faced with questions like these, many Christians know only two options. One is to bite your tongue while your heart slowly freezes over. The other is to say everything on your mind—and when you’re done, the relationship is broken. Paul offers a third way: “speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ” (Ephesians 4:15).

“Speaking truth” is more than saying true things. It means living in the truth and holding fast to it, the very opposite of being carried about “by the trickery of men, in craftiness” in the verse before (see Ephesians 4:14). God doesn’t want us to pretend to agree, because false harmony isn’t unity—it’s just silence. Yet Paul places truthfulness inside love. Love is the soil our words grow in; truth is the fruit that grows from it. Truth without love is like a blade without a handle: both the one who holds it and the one it strikes end up bleeding. Love without truth is like a sugar-coated pill with no medicine inside: sweet, but it cures nothing.

The Old Testament already knew this wisdom: “Better is open rebuke than hidden love. The wounds of a friend are faithful” (Proverbs 27:5-6). God wants words spoken face to face, out of faithfulness—not muttering behind someone’s back.

Even more important is the direction of this verse: “into him who is the head, Christ.” When I voice a different opinion, my goal isn’t to win or to prove I’m right. It is to help the body look more like its head. When two members both turn toward the head, a disagreement stops being a tug-of-war and becomes a way of correcting one another. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on your heart: Is the thing I disagree with about letting Christ grow—or about letting me grow?
lessons.light: When self-centered people disagree, the focus is “Am I right?” When selfless people disagree, the focus is “Is Christ being lifted up?” Pride provokes pride; two people who both want to win will both lose. Humility draws out humility; two people who both turn to the head can both win. Speaking truth in love means letting Jesus reign over my lips.
think: In Ephesians 4:14-16, where is “speaking truth” ultimately meant to lead us?
When I face a disagreement, do I tend to hold it in or let it all out?
How can I bring the disagreement in my heart to the head first?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the truth, and you are love. I confess that I often either go silent until I grow cold, or speak until I wound. Holy Spirit, govern my heart and my tongue. Let every true word I speak be soaked in love, and let my goal be not to win, but to help your body look more like you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down one recent thing at church you disagree with. Beside it, make two columns: “The truth I want to say” and “My love for this person.” Tonight, pray one minute for the issue and one minute for the person.
lessons.quick: Don’t fake agreement or wound with words—speak the truth in love.
text: that we may no longer be children, tossed back and forth and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the trickery of men, in craftiness, after the wiles of error;
but speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ,

from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.

lessons.title: The Church’s First Great Debate
lessons.hear:
One church’s ministry team spent three full months debating whether to keep online Sunday services after the pandemic. An elder worried that online gatherings were making people casual about church. A group of younger co-workers argued that for many people living far from home, it was their only spiritual family. Around the meeting table everyone was polite, but afterward their separate group chats were buzzing. Some began to wonder, “How can a spiritual church have so many arguments? Is something wrong with us?”

That is an old mindset many of us carry: a good church shouldn’t have disagreements. But look at the early church. The Holy Spirit had just been poured out, the apostles were still alive—and yet a dispute erupted over the very heart of the gospel: Did Gentiles have to be circumcised to be saved? Luke doesn’t hide it. Paul and Barnabas “had no small discord and discussion with them” (Acts 15:2).

God’s perspective is this: an argument in itself is not failure; how we handle it reveals what we’re really made of. The church in Jerusalem did three things. First, they brought the issue into the open, taking it to the apostles and elders instead of quietly lobbying for votes. Second, they listened to one another. Peter told how God had given the Holy Spirit to the Gentiles; then “all the multitude kept silence, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul” (Acts 15:12); and James confirmed it with the words of the prophets. Third, they sought the Holy Spirit’s mind together, so their conclusion reads, “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us” (Acts 15:28).

That church eventually learned too. They stopped the crossfire in their group chats and set aside two evenings just to listen, not to debate. The older members shared their worry about people drifting; the younger ones shared their burden for members far away. The final decision wasn’t about who won. It was an arrangement in which both sides could see the Lord’s heart. Disagreement is not the enemy of unity; pride and private factions are.
lessons.light: The old mindset says unity means no disagreement. God’s perspective says unity is people who disagree submitting together under the head. In the words “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us” (Acts 15:28), the Holy Spirit comes first and we come second. That is the order of letting Jesus reign, and what it really looks like for the Holy Spirit to be my guide.
think: In Acts 15:1-12, what methods did the church use to handle this dispute?
Do I assume that a church with arguments must be unspiritual?
The next time there’s disagreement in a ministry meeting or small group, whom will I listen to first?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for recording even the early church’s arguments in Scripture, so I can know that your house is not a house without differences, but a house that keeps seeking you in the midst of them. Take away my desire to win and give me ears that listen. In every discussion, let the Holy Spirit’s will go ahead of my opinions. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a co-worker or church member who sees things differently from you. Today, invite them for tea or give them a call, and begin by asking, “What’s the burden behind the way you see this?” Only listen—don’t argue—and thank them when they’re done.
lessons.quick: Arguments aren’t failure; how we handle them shows who we really are.
text: Some men came down from Judea and taught the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised after the custom of Moses, you can’t be saved.”

Therefore when Paul and Barnabas had no small discord and discussion with them, they appointed Paul, Barnabas, and some others of them to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question.
They, being sent on their way by the assembly, passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, declaring the conversion of the Gentiles. They caused great joy to all the brothers.
When they had come to Jerusalem, they were received by the assembly and the apostles and the elders, and they reported everything that God had done with them.
But some of the sect of the Pharisees who believed rose up, saying, “It is necessary to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.”
The apostles and the elders were gathered together to see about this matter.

When there had been much discussion, Peter rose up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that a good while ago God made a choice among you that by my mouth the nations should hear the word of the Good News and believe.
God, who knows the heart, testified about them, giving them the Holy Spirit, just like he did to us.
He made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith.
Now therefore why do you tempt God, that you should put a yoke on the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?
But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.”
All the multitude kept silence, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul reporting what signs and wonders God had done among the nations through them.

lessons.title: Go to Them, Not to Others
lessons.hear:
In church hallways you often hear a certain line: “I’ll tell you, but don’t tell anyone else…” What follows is usually about a ministry leader, a pastor, or a decision. The speaker feels they’re just venting; the listener feels trusted. But the moment those words are spoken, the body of Christ gains another invisible crack.

Proverbs puts it sharply: “A perverse man stirs up strife. A whisperer separates close friends” (Proverbs 16:28). And again: “For lack of wood a fire goes out. Without gossip, a quarrel dies down” (Proverbs 26:20). Talking behind someone’s back adds wood to the fire; forming a faction piles the wood into a mountain.

Jesus gives us the opposite path: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother” (Matthew 18:15). Notice three details. It says “go”—I am the one who takes the initiative. It says “between you and him alone”—not first gathering a few friends to weigh in. And the goal is to have “gained back your brother,” not to win a court case. If he won’t listen, take one or two others; if he still won’t listen, then tell the church. Every step aims at restoration, not a public trial.

Today’s practice has three moves. 1. Stop: when you want to tell a third person what’s wrong with someone, pause and ask, “Does this person even know I have a problem with them?” 2. Go: if it’s worth saying, go to the person directly, privately, and gently. 3. Block: when someone comes to you to talk about another member, say gently, “Have you talked with them about this yourself? Would you like me to go with you?”

This takes courage. But that courage can save a relationship—and protect the whole body.
lessons.light: Talking behind someone’s back is the self-centered shortcut: I don’t have to face anyone, and I still get to look right. The selfless path is narrower, but it leads to life: first with God, then with people; first bring your words to the Lord, then to the person involved. People matter more than issues—the purpose of speaking is always to have “gained back your brother” (Matthew 18:15).
think: In Matthew 18:15-17, what is the purpose of each step?
Have I recently talked about a church member or co-worker behind their back?
Whom do I need to go to directly? How will I begin the conversation?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I often say to others what I should say to one person. Forgive me for letting my tongue crack your body. Give me courage to go directly, gentleness to speak privately, and wisdom to stop rumors. May my words become a bridge of reconciliation, not wood for the fire of division. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If there’s something you’ve complained about to others, pray first today, then privately and gently arrange to talk with the person involved. Also tell the one who heard your complaint, “What I said last time wasn’t fair. I’m going to talk to them directly.”
lessons.quick: If you have something to say, go to the person—not to a third party.
text: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.
But if he doesn’t listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.
If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly. If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.

lessons.title: Facing Up or Slipping Away
lessons.hear:
Something deeply embarrassing once happened in the church at Antioch. The apostle Peter had been eating at the same table as Gentile believers. But when certain people arrived from Jerusalem, “he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision” (Galatians 2:12). The other Jewish believers joined him in his hypocrisy, and even Barnabas, always so generous, was carried away. One man’s fear drew a dividing line right through the church.

This passage holds up two mirrors. The first is Peter. He didn’t publicly oppose anyone; he just quietly changed seats. But his withdrawal was itself a kind of faction-making—an action that said, “We’re on this side, and they’re on that side.” We can do the same. We don’t say anything bad, but we only eat with the same circle, only share our opinions in front of certain people, and line up our votes privately before the meeting.

The second mirror is Paul: “I resisted him to his face” (Galatians 2:11). He didn’t write an anonymous letter or organize an opposition party behind Peter’s back. He directly and openly confronted something that had already publicly distorted the truth of the gospel. This wasn’t temper; it was faithfulness—to the gospel, and to Peter.

Look honestly at yourself. When I disagree, am I more like Peter, pulling away instead of talking? Like Barnabas, following the crowd instead of the truth? Or can I be like Paul, speaking face to face at the right time and in the right way?

Here is the grace: the story doesn’t end there. Years later, Peter wrote of “our beloved brother Paul” (2 Peter 3:15). The man who was confronted to his face still called his confronter a beloved brother. When truth is spoken in love, even a wound can heal into a deeper bond.
lessons.light: Peter withdrew because he feared people—and the fear of people is really self-centeredness, because what I care about most is my own image and safety. The way to adjust is to return to my proper place: I am the Lord’s servant, not the spokesperson of a faction. Change begins with me. Only when I step out of my own little circle can I call the church to unity.
think: In Galatians 2:11-14, whom did Peter’s withdrawal affect?
Have I, intentionally or not, formed a little circle at church?
What concrete action will I take to erase one dividing line?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that sometimes I’m like Peter, afraid of people and pulling away instead of being honest; and sometimes like Barnabas, carried along by the loudest voices. Search my heart and tear down the cliques and factions inside me. Give me courage to speak the truth face to face at the right time, and humility to receive correction when it comes to me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This Sunday or at your next small group, deliberately sit next to someone you rarely interact with—perhaps someone you’ve disagreed with. Greet them first and spend five minutes asking how they’re doing.
lessons.quick: Don’t slip away or follow the hypocrisy; speak face to face in love.
text: But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned.
For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision.
And the rest of the Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy.

But when I saw that they didn’t walk uprightly according to the truth of the Good News, I said to Peter before them all, “If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do, and not as the Jews do, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews do?

lessons.title: The Right Path When Wrong Is Serious
lessons.hear:
This week we’ve learned that when we disagree, we speak the truth in love; when someone sins against us, we go to them privately first; and we don’t form factions or talk behind people’s backs. But one more situation needs to be made clear. What if the problem isn’t a difference of opinion, but serious wrongdoing—spiritual manipulation and abuse of power, sexual harassment, violence, financial dishonesty?

Scripture never asks people to stay silent for the sake of “unity.” Paul instructed Timothy, “Don’t receive an accusation against an elder, except at the word of two or three witnesses” (1 Timothy 5:19). On one hand, this protects leaders from slander and rumor. On the other hand, it makes clear that accusations against leaders can—and should—be formally handled. And those who handle them must “observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality” (1 Timothy 5:21).

So keep a three-level map in mind. 1. Differences of opinion: speak the truth in love, express your view through proper channels, and in the end respect the decision the community reaches in prayer. 2.
