Personal offenses: follow the Lord’s instructions—first privately, then with witnesses, then tell the church. 3. Serious wrongdoing: the person who has been harmed does not need to confront the more powerful party alone first. Find a trustworthy third party—the elders and deacons board, the church’s denomination or oversight body, professional counselors and advocates—and when the law has been broken, seek legal protection. Giving an honest account to those responsible is completely different from spreading the story around. The first lets light into the darkness; only the second is gossip. Those who have been harmed should never have to swallow the harm to protect the church’s reputation.

This week, share this three-level map with your small group or a spiritual companion. A church that knows how to handle disagreement in love, and has the courage to face serious wrongdoing with justice, is a home where people can feel safe.
lessons.light: Letting Jesus reign includes letting his justice and his light reign. Proud power tends to cover things up; a humble church dares to face them. Protecting those who have been hurt is protecting the body of Christ. This doesn’t destroy unity; it removes the cancer that destroys unity, so that God’s name is honored as holy.
think: What principles for handling accusations does 1 Timothy 5:19-21 give?
Have I ever used “unity” as an excuse not to face a problem?
With whom will I share this week’s three-level map, and when?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are light, and in you there is no darkness at all. Make our church able both to hold differences of opinion in love and to face serious wrongdoing with justice. Protect those who are weak and wounded, and let them find safety in your house. Make me a member of your body who speaks the truth, guards my tongue, and loves my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write the three-level approach—differences of opinion, personal offenses, serious wrongdoing—on a small card. Send it to your spiritual companion or small group, and agree together: we won’t talk about others behind their backs.
lessons.quick: Disagree openly, resolve offenses privately, and take serious wrongs to a trusted third party.
text: Don’t receive an accusation against an elder except at the word of two or three witnesses.
Those who sin, reprove in the sight of all, that the rest also may be in fear.
I command you in the sight of God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, and the chosen angels, that you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing by partiality.

weeks.title: Becoming Co-Workers and Examples
weeks.keyText: Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.
weeks.theme: From being shepherded to shepherding together: I follow Christ, and others can follow me as I follow him.
group: Read 1 Corinthians 11:1 and 1 Timothy 4:12. Does “being an example” feel like pressure or hope to you? Why?
Who has been an example or co-worker in your faith? What did they do that shaped you?
This week, let each of us name one behind-the-scenes co-worker we want to thank, and let’s write them a thank-you card together.
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, arrive ten minutes early and notice the people who were preparing long before you came: sound, welcome, children’s ministry, cleaning. Pray for them during the service. Afterward, find one of them, thank them specifically, and ask, “Is there anything I could help with alongside you?”

lessons.title: Imitate Me as I Imitate Christ
lessons.hear:
Paul once said something very bold: “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). If someone said that from the pulpit today, we might frown: Isn’t that rather arrogant? But look closely at how the sentence is built. The first half is an invitation; the second half is a boundary. Paul isn’t asking people to copy his personality, his eloquence, or his achievements, but the part of him that imitates Christ. He is like a mirror, and a mirror’s value isn’t in itself but in the face it reflects.

That is how the church in Thessalonica grew. Paul says the gospel came to them “not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 1:5), and they saw with their own eyes how Paul lived among them. As a result, “You became imitators of us, and of the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 1:6), and then “you became an example to all who believe in Macedonia and in Achaia” (1 Thessalonians 1:7).

This is a chain of life passed hand to hand: Christ, then Paul, then the Thessalonians, then the believers of Macedonia and Achaia. Faith isn’t only a body of doctrine to be preached; it is a way of life to be seen and imitated. A church grows not only through words from the pulpit, but through visible lives, one after another, among its members.

So the question isn’t “Am I good enough to be an example?” You already are an example in someone’s eyes—either a good one or a bad one. Your children, the newcomer in your small group, your colleagues are all watching how you face hardship, how you speak, and how you treat serving. God’s heart is to move you from being someone who is shepherded to someone who works alongside the pastors and shepherds together with them.
lessons.light: An example isn’t perfection; it’s direction. A selfless example leads people to Christ; a self-centered example keeps people focused on itself. The first of our three foundations is “Jesus is my example.” As I imitate him, I also become a visible witness to the “2” around me—this is exactly the practice of 920.
think: In 1 Thessalonians 1:5-8, how was the gospel passed on from one place to the next?
Whose life has made me want to follow Christ more? And in whose eyes am I an example?
What detail of my daily life this week do I want people to see Christ in?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are my example. Thank you for bringing me to yourself through the lives of so many brothers and sisters. Today I also want to be a visible witness to others—not because I am perfect, but because I am following you. Holy Spirit, prune me, so that what people see in me is not me, but you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to someone who has influenced your faith. Tell them specifically which way they imitated Christ that taught you to follow the Lord too.
lessons.quick: An example isn’t perfection; it’s a direction that points people to Christ.
text: and that our Good News came to you not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit and with much assurance. You know what kind of men we showed ourselves to be among you for your sake.
You became imitators of us and of the Lord, having received the word in much affliction, with joy of the Holy Spirit,
so that you became an example to all who believe in Macedonia and in Achaia.
For from you the word of the Lord has been declared, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward God has gone out, so that we need not say anything.

lessons.title: Timothy, Like-Minded with Me
lessons.hear:
A young mother sat quietly in her small group for two years. She often said, “If I can take care of my kids and get to church on time on Sunday, that’s already pretty good. Serving is for the spiritual people.” Then one day her small group leader asked her to help care for a newcomer who also had toddlers. All she did was send one message a week and occasionally share a parenting tip. Six months later, when that newcomer was baptized, she said, “She made me feel there was someone in the church who understood me.” That day the young mother realized: being a co-worker isn’t a job title; it’s a heart.

Many people hold an old mindset: serving is for pastors and a handful of ministry workers; I’m just a member being cared for. Yet when Paul describes Timothy, he doesn’t use a title. He describes a heart: “For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you. For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:20-21).

Timothy wasn’t a co-worker from the start. He was a young disciple from Lystra (see Acts 16:1-2) whom Paul took along, and who learned by watching. Paul says, “as a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News” (Philippians 2:22). From a son being led to a co-worker laboring alongside his father—this is the path God wants every believer to walk.

A co-worker has three marks. Like-minded: aligned with the heart of the Lord and of those who lead. Caring: truly concerned about other people’s lives. Not self-seeking: focused on the things of Christ. None of these requires a theology degree or a pulpit. If today you begin to truly care about one member of the body, and to share the church’s direction, you are already standing in the ranks of co-workers.
lessons.light: “They all seek their own” (Philippians 2:21) describes the self-centered life; a co-worker’s heart is self-denying: for Jesus, for others, not for myself. Moving from being shepherded to shepherding together is a change in ministry that flows from a change of life—first life, then relationships, then ministry. We don’t wait to receive a position before we start loving people.
think: In Philippians 2:19-24, what words does Paul use to describe Timothy?
Do I feel that serving has nothing to do with me? What is the reason behind that?
In what area can I be like-minded with the church and truly care for someone?
lessons.speak: Father, forgive me for so often thinking that serving is someone else’s job, wanting only to be fed and cared for. Give me Timothy’s heart: like-minded with you, caring for others, not seeking my own. Move me from sitting in the pews to laboring alongside the pastors and my brothers and sisters as a co-worker. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask your small group leader or a ministry team member, “Is there one small thing I could help with this month?” Then take one on—for example, regularly caring for a newcomer.
lessons.quick: A co-worker isn’t a title; it’s being like-minded, caring, and not self-seeking.
text: But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered up when I know how you are doing.
For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you.
For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.
But you know that he has proved himself. As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News.
Therefore I hope to send him at once, as soon as I see how it will go with me.
But I trust in the Lord that I myself also will come shortly.

lessons.title: A Thank-You List Full of Names
lessons.hear:
Many people reading Romans skip chapter 16—a long list of unfamiliar names that seems to have nothing to do with us. But this chapter is actually a thank-you list Paul wrote, and a group portrait of the early church’s co-workers.

First he commends a sister named Phoebe, saying “she herself also has been a helper of many, and of my own self” (Romans 16:2). Then he greets Prisca and Aquila, “my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their own necks for my life” (Romans 16:3-4)—and a church met in their home. He also mentions a woman named Mary, “who labored much for us” (Romans 16:6). Most of these people left behind no sermons and built no large churches, yet the Holy Spirit recorded them in Scripture one by one.

This passage gives us two lessons we can practice today.

First, notice your co-workers and say their names. Paul doesn’t say a vague “thanks, everyone.” He names who did what. Your church has its Phoebes too: the sound volunteer who is first to arrive and last to leave every week; the sister who quietly tidies the children’s classroom; the care team member who remembers every senior’s birthday. Today, thank one of them specifically.

Second, become a name on someone else’s list. What Prisca and Aquila did was ordinary: they opened their home, welcomed people, and walked alongside them. You don’t have to start on the stage. You just need to be willing to open your time, your dinner table, and your hands, and become a co-worker someone in the body can lean on.

God does not forget the love we show for his name (see Hebrews 6:10). May you be remembered—not because you are famous, but because you are faithful.
lessons.light: People matter more than tasks. What Paul remembered wasn’t how grand the events were, but the names of his co-workers, one by one. Selfless co-workers don’t care whether they are seen, but they love to see others. In a church like that, the glory goes to God, not to any star.
think: In Romans 16:1-7, what specific things does Paul praise his co-workers for?
Do I only notice the people up front and overlook the co-workers serving quietly?
For which member of the body can I become a Prisca and Aquila?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for remembering every co-worker who quietly gives. Open my eyes to see the Phoebes, Priscas, and Aquilas around me, and to thank them with specific words. Use my ordinary home, my time, and my hands to make me a faithful co-worker in your kingdom. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write a specific thank-you card or message to a behind-the-scenes co-worker. Say what they did and how it helped you, and pray for their ministry.
lessons.quick: Notice the names of your co-workers, and become a co-worker on someone else’s list.
text: I commend to you Phoebe, our sister, who is a servant of the assembly that is at Cenchreae,
that you receive her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and that you assist her in whatever matter she may need from you, for she herself also has been a helper of many, and of my own self.
Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus,
who risked their own necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the assemblies of the Gentiles.
Greet the assembly that is in their house. Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the first fruits of Achaia to Christ.
Greet Mary, who labored much for us.
Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and my fellow prisoners, who are notable among the apostles, who were also in Christ before me.

lessons.title: Mark, Once Given Up On
lessons.hear:
John Mark was once part of Paul and Barnabas’s mission team, but he left partway through, in Pamphylia (see Acts 13:13). Later, Barnabas wanted to take him along again, and Paul firmly refused. “Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other” (Acts 15:39).

Scripture doesn’t judge who was right or wrong. Paul took the seriousness of the mission to heart; Barnabas took a person’s restoration to heart. Both were good co-workers, yet they couldn’t walk together on this matter. But God did something wonderful here: one team became two. Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus, and Paul took Silas to strengthen the churches. God didn’t stop his work because his co-workers were imperfect.

The ending is even more moving. Years later, writing to Timothy from prison, Paul said, “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). The young man once considered not worth taking became Paul’s helper in his final years.

This story invites us to examine ourselves from three angles. If you are Mark: Have you stepped back from serving after one failure or one criticism, and never dared to return? God’s grace is bigger than your failure. If you are Paul: Are you too quick to label someone “unreliable” and refuse them a second chance? Those who set an example must also learn to see others’ growth. If you are Barnabas: Are you willing to walk with a co-worker who has fallen until they stand again?

The way to adjust is to peel off the labels and open the door again. A true ministry team isn’t made up of people who never fail, but of people who are willing to restore one another.
lessons.light: Self-centered co-workers hide when they fail and shut others out when they fail. Selfless co-workers accept themselves in grace and welcome others in grace. When Paul later said Mark was “useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11), it was the most beautiful adjustment an example can make: admitting that God’s work in someone else was bigger than my earlier judgment.
think: In Acts 15:36-41, what did Paul and Barnabas each value?
When it comes to failure and restoration in ministry, am I more like Mark, Paul, or Barnabas?
Which co-worker needs me to peel off a label and give them another chance?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that you didn’t give up on Mark because of his failure, and you haven’t given up on me because of mine. Heal the discouragement I’ve suffered in serving, and help me stand up again. Forgive me for the labels I’ve put on others. Make me like Barnabas, walking with a fallen co-worker as they set out once more. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of someone who stepped back from serving, or whom you decided wasn’t suitable. Reach out to them today, say one specific word of affirmation, and invite them to do a small act of service with you.
lessons.quick: Failure isn’t the end of a co-worker; restoring one another is a team’s strength.
text: After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.”
Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.
He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.

lessons.title: An Example to the Believers
lessons.hear:
“Let no man despise your youth”—young people often take these words as a motto. But read the rest of the sentence: “be an example to those who believe, in word, in your way of life, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity” (1 Timothy 4:12). The way not to be looked down on isn’t to fight for a voice; it is to live a life others can see.

The areas Paul lists cover the whole of life. Word is how I speak. Way of life is how I act. Love is how I treat people. Spirit is the inner posture of my heart. Faith is how I face hardship. Purity is how I live when no one is watching. Then he says, “Be diligent in these things. Give yourself wholly to them, that your progress may be revealed to all” (1 Timothy 4:15). Notice: progress, not perfection. An example isn’t a bronze statue that never moves; it’s a life that is still growing.

This week we’ve walked a path: imitating those who imitate Christ; moving from being shepherded to being a like-minded co-worker; noticing and thanking other co-workers; restoring one another after failure. The last step is to hand this path on to the next person. In the Old Testament, God told Moses, “But commission Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him” (Deuteronomy 3:28). Later Moses laid his hands on Joshua, and the Israelites listened to him (see Deuteronomy 34:9). What Moses left behind wasn’t only the years he led, but a person to carry on.

There is surely a Joshua in your life too: a newcomer in your small group, a teenager at church, a co-worker who has just started serving. Choose one person today and walk with them for a while. You don’t have to wait until you are fully ready. You only need to be a few steps ahead of them, with your eyes always fixed on Christ.
lessons.light: The “3” in 235 is the relationship of spiritual parents and children: I am led by someone, and I lead someone else. Multiplying isn’t copying myself; it’s helping others imitate Christ. When I’m glad to see the next generation become stronger than me, that is selflessness—the glory doesn’t go to me, but to God.
think: In 1 Timothy 4:12-16, in what areas is Timothy to be an example?
Of these areas, where do I most need to grow?
Who is the Joshua I will walk with? What will my first step be?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for showing me this week that I am not only someone to be shepherded, but someone called to be a co-worker and an example. Help me grow in word, in my way of life, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity. Give me someone to walk alongside, so that your life can be passed on through me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose someone who came to faith after you or has just started serving. Invite them to share a meal or read the Bible together this week, and ask, “Is there anything in your faith you’d like us to learn together?”
lessons.quick: An example isn’t perfection but visible growth; pass your life on to the next person.
text: Let no man despise your youth; but be an example to those who believe, in word, in your way of life, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity.
Until I come, pay attention to reading, to exhortation, and to teaching.
Don’t neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you by prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the elders.
Be diligent in these things. Give yourself wholly to them, that your progress may be revealed to all.
Pay attention to yourself and to your teaching. Continue in these things, for in doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

weeks.title: A New Commandment: Love One Another
weeks.keyText: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
weeks.theme: Loving one another isn’t something we do when we have spare time; it is the Lord’s command and the mark of his disciples.
group: Read John 13:34-35. How is Jesus’ love different from what people usually mean by love?
Who has loved you in a concrete way at church? How did that affect you?
This week we begin a “love relay”: each of us will love one member of the body in a concrete way and share about it next time we meet.
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, notice who arrives alone, sits alone, and leaves alone. Before the service, ask the Lord for eyes that really see people. During the service, quietly pray for that person. Afterward, walk over and greet them, and invite them to lunch—or at least chat for five minutes. Let “if you have love for one another” (John 13:35) become real today.

lessons.title: A New Commandment
lessons.hear:
It was the night Jesus was betrayed. He had just bent down to wash his disciples’ feet, and Judas had just walked out into the night. At that very moment, Jesus left a command that sounds like a final testament: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another” (John 13:34).

The strange thing is that love wasn’t new. Back in the law of Moses, God had commanded, “You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). So what was new?

The measure was new. The Old Testament’s measure was “as yourself”—love others the way you love yourself. Jesus’ measure is “just as I have loved you.” He loved disciples who argued about who was greatest, who stumbled, who would deny him. His love bent down to wash feet and finally walked to the cross. That measure is far higher, and far deeper, than “as yourself.”

The source was new. We don’t squeeze love out of ourselves; we are loved by him first, and that is what enables us to love. Love is like water: it has to flow in from the source before it can flow out through us.

The witness was new. “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). Jesus didn’t say the world would recognize us by our buildings, programs, doctrines, or gifts, but by our love for one another. How church members treat each other is the first gospel the world reads.

So loving one another isn’t an extra-credit question we get to when we have spare time after meetings and ministry. It is the Lord’s command and the mark of his disciples. Today, ask the Holy Spirit first to let you feel afresh how the Lord loves you, and then let that love flow to the brothers and sisters around you.
lessons.light: From a human point of view, love is a feeling: if I have it, I give it; if not, never mind. From God’s point of view, love is a command, because the source of love isn’t me—it’s Christ. Rely on the Spirit with your heart rather than on yourself with your head. When I abide in the Lord’s love, loving one another goes from “I can’t” to “Christ lives in me.”
think: In John 13:34-35, what is “new” about this commandment?
Do I treat loving one another as something I do when I have spare time?
Today, whom in the body can I love the way the Lord has loved me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, on the night you were betrayed, you still loved your disciples to the end. Thank you for loving me that way too. Fill me first with your love, then let it flow to the brothers and sisters around me, so that when people see us loving one another, they will know we are your disciples. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, spend five quiet minutes remembering a concrete way the Lord has loved you. Then love someone in the same way. For example, if the Lord once sent someone to be with you when you were weak, go and be with someone today.
lessons.quick: As the Lord loves me, I love my brothers and sisters.
text: When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him.
If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and he will glorify him immediately.
Little children, I will be with you a little while longer. You will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you can’t come,’ so now I tell you.
A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

lessons.title: Not Only in Word or Tongue
lessons.hear:
A brother in a small group lost his job. The night he shared the news in the group chat, messages poured in one after another: “Hang in there!” “Praying for you!” “God will provide!”—along with plenty of praying-hands emojis. He was grateful. But that week his fridge stayed empty, and no one helped him look over his résumé. Then a retired sister showed up at his door with a bag of groceries and spent an afternoon helping him revise his résumé. Later he said, “That bag of groceries was the first time I knew for sure that the church really loved me.”

Many people hold an old mindset: love is a feeling; if it’s in your heart, that’s enough; if you don’t feel it, don’t force it. But John sees it completely differently: “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18).

John nails the definition of love to the cross: “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (1 John 3:16). The essence of love isn’t “I feel,” but “I give.” Then he gets very specific, even uncomfortably so: if someone has the world’s goods, sees a brother in need, and closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him? (see 1 John 3:17).

John even says that loving the brothers is how we know we have passed out of death into life (see 1 John 3:14). This doesn’t mean we are saved by loving. It means that anyone truly touched by God’s life will grow acts of love, just as a living tree will grow leaves.

Those emojis weren’t wrong, and prayer is precious. But love that stays on the tongue is like a letter written and never mailed. God wants us to mail the letter.
lessons.light: Love that stays a feeling is centered on me: Do I feel like it? Is it convenient for me? Love that moves into action is centered on the other person: What do they need? Self-denial means living for Jesus, for others, not for myself. When life is changed, our living and our relationships change with it.
think: In 1 John 3:16-18, how does John define love?
Does my love usually stop at words, or does it show up in action?
Who around me in the body has a practical need right now?
lessons.speak: Father, forgive me for so often loving people only with my mouth—sending emojis instead of showing up, ending my concern with a promise to pray. Open my closed heart of compassion, and teach me to be like Jesus, turning love into deed and truth. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, find a member of the body who is going through a practical hardship. Besides praying for them, do one concrete thing: bring a meal, help with a task, or spend half an hour with them.
lessons.quick: Love doesn’t only say “I’m praying for you”; it shows up with a bag of groceries.
text: For this is the message which you heard from the beginning, that we should love one another—
unlike Cain, who was of the evil one and killed his brother. Why did he kill him? Because his deeds were evil, and his brother’s righteous.
Don’t be surprised, my brothers, if the world hates you.
We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers. He who doesn’t love his brother remains in death.
Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him.
By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.
But whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, then closes his heart of compassion against him, how does God’s love remain in him?
My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.

lessons.title: The Debt of Love We Never Finish Paying
lessons.hear:
Many of us in Chinese culture hate owing anyone a favor. Receive a gift, and we start thinking about when to give one back. Someone treats us to a meal, and next time we fight to pick up the bill. We want the ledger of favors to be settled, so no one owes anyone anything.

But Paul says something remarkable: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Romans 13:8). Every other debt should be paid off; the debt of love is the one we never finish paying. Why? Because the love we have received from God is infinite. How can someone who has been forgiven a debt of millions count every last cent with a brother?

This verse overturns the ledger mentality we often bring into church: “I helped him last time; this time it’s his turn to help me.” “She never checks on me—why should I check on her?” Once love becomes an exchange, it is no longer love; it’s business.

Paul also says, “Love doesn’t harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law” (Romans 13:10). That gives us a very practical place to start. Today, choose one member of the body and make one installment payment on your debt of love:

1. Speak one specific word of affirmation: not just “You’re great,” but “The song you led last week really comforted me.” 2. Do one thing that expects nothing in return: pick up their kids, cover a shift for them, drive them home. 3. Keep one act of “no harm”: when you want to say something that would sting, or post a snide reply in the group chat, choose not to.

The more you pay on this debt, the richer your heart becomes. Every time you give, you are drawing from the Lord’s infinite love—an account that will never be overdrawn.
lessons.light: Self-centered people live by the ledger, calculating who owes whom. Selfless people live by grace, remembering that what they owe the Lord is a love they can never repay. Relationships matter more than things. The church isn’t a place to trade favors; it’s a place where God’s love circulates.
think: In Romans 13:8-10, how are love and the law related?
Is there a hidden ledger of favors in my relationships at church?
To whom will I make an installment payment of love today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, what I owe you is a love I can never repay. Forgive me for still keeping score at church, remembering who did what for me and who didn’t. Today make me willing to love one member of the body freely, expecting nothing back: to affirm them with my words, help them with my actions, and do them no harm with my tongue. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, do three things for the same person: one specific word of affirmation, one act of help that expects nothing in return, and one snide remark you hold back. Before bed, write down how it went in your journal.
lessons.quick: Pay off every other debt, but keep owing the debt of love.
text: Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.

For the commandments, “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and whatever other commandments there are, are all summed up in this saying, namely, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
Love doesn’t harm a neighbor. Love therefore is the fulfillment of the law.

lessons.title: Do You Love Me?
lessons.hear:
Peter once swore to Jesus, “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:37). A few hours later, in the high priest’s courtyard, a servant girl at the door asked whether he was one of Jesus’ disciples. He said, “I am not” (John 18:17). The one who declared his love was the same one who denied him.

By the Sea of Galilee, the risen Lord prepared a charcoal fire and breakfast, and then asked Peter three times: Do you love me? He didn’t ask, “Why did you deny me?” He didn’t bring up the past. He simply probed, gently and deeply, at the root of Peter’s love. Each time Peter answered, “You know that I have affection for you,” Jesus followed with a charge to care for his flock, ending with, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). The Lord tied loving him to caring for his sheep.

This holds up a mirror for us. Our love for our brothers and sisters often fails, and behind the failure are some familiar self-centered patterns. We love only the lovable and keep our distance from difficult people. We love until we get hurt, then pull back and go cold. Or we turn love into control—“I’m doing this for your own good, so you need to listen to me.” John puts it bluntly: “he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” (1 John 4:20). The temperature between me and my brother actually reflects the temperature between me and the Lord.

The way to adjust isn’t to grit our teeth and try harder. It is to return, like Peter, to the charcoal fire and let the Lord ask you again: Do you love me? When you are touched afresh by his love, you’ll find that the difficult person is also one of the Lord’s sheep—someone he has entrusted to you to love.

Peter went on to become an apostle who shepherded the flock. His failure didn’t disqualify him; it taught him that love doesn’t run on our own enthusiasm, but on the Lord’s grace.
lessons.light: Peter failed because he declared his love in his own enthusiasm; he was restored when he came back to the Lord to be loved. The focus is on Jesus—not on myself, and not on the person who is hard to love. The order of relationships is first with God, then with people. When my relationship with the Lord is set right, my love for my brothers and sisters has a source.
think: In John 21:15-17, how does Jesus connect loving him with caring for his sheep?
In what kinds of situations am I most likely to withdraw my love from someone in the body?
Which difficult member of the body is a sheep the Lord wants me to love again?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, like Peter, I have loudly declared my love and then shrunk back when things got hard. Thank you for not bringing up my past, but asking me once more: Do you love me? Lord, you know that I love you. Let this love flow to the person I find so hard to love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down the name of someone from whom you’ve withdrawn your love. Pray for them three times today, each time asking the Lord, “How do you want me to feed this sheep?” Then write down one small step you can take.
lessons.quick: Come back to the Lord’s fire to be loved, and you can love the hard-to-love again.
text: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

lessons.title: God Remains in Us
lessons.hear:
John says honestly that no one has ever seen God. We can’t see God, and the world can see him even less. But then he says, “No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us” (1 John 4:12). The invisible God chooses to be seen through the visible love we have for one another.

This week we began with the new commandment Jesus gave on the night he was betrayed, and saw that love’s new measure is “just as I have loved you.” We learned that love is not only in word, but in deed and truth. We made an installment payment on a debt of love we’ll never finish paying. And by the charcoal fire, we were restored by the Lord. Now it’s time to let that love multiply.

The Old Testament tells of a moving friendship: “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul” (1 Samuel 18:1). Humanly speaking, Jonathan was the prince, and David might take his throne. But Jonathan chose love and covenant over rivalry. Churches often have similar situations: two co-workers in the same ministry, or two families in the same small group, who could easily compare themselves with each other, but who instead become a blessing to each other because of love.

Love is passed on. A member of the body who has been loved in a concrete way becomes more able to love others. So this week’s multiplication is simple: tell one person a story of how you were loved or how you loved someone this week, and invite them to go and love someone too. If a small group keeps a love relay like this going every week, it won’t need big events—the church will become a home people want to stay in.

John’s words are worth reading again and again: “Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another” (1 John 4:11).
lessons.light: Multiplying doesn’t mean preaching more about love; it means passing on stories of love. The “9” in 920 is the fruit of the Spirit, and the first fruit listed is love (see Galatians 5:22). When that fruit grows in me, the “2” around me will get a taste of God. Love comes from God, and all the glory goes to him.
think: In 1 John 4:7-12, where does love come from, and what does loving one another bring about?
This week, where did I experience being loved or loving someone?
To whom will I tell my story of love, and whom will I invite them to love?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for loving us first and sending your Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. This week you have taught me that loving one another is your command and the mark of your disciples. Make our small group and our church a place where you can be seen, and let love be passed on among us from one person to the next. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, share one experience from this week of being loved or loving someone—in three to five sentences—with your spiritual companion or small group, and invite them to love one member of the body in a concrete way this week.
lessons.quick: The invisible God is seen through our love for one another.
text: Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.
He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love.
By this God’s love was revealed in us, that God has sent his only born Son into the world that we might live through him.
In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we also ought to love one another.
No one has seen God at any time. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love has been perfected in us.

weeks.title: Bearing and Accepting One Another
weeks.keyText: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
weeks.theme: Carry the burdens fellow members can’t carry alone, and accept those who are different from me, just as Christ accepted me.
group: Read Galatians 6:2 and Romans 15:7. What do “bearing” and “accepting” each look like in your life?
Have you ever been accepted or carried by members of a different generation or background? Share that experience.
This week, let’s divide up practical help for a member who is carrying a heavy burden—each of us will take on one task.
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, look for someone in the congregation from a different generation or background, and sit near them to worship together. As you sing, imagine the great choir of every nation and tribe before the throne. After the service, greet them and ask, “Is there anything I can pray for you about this week?”

lessons.title: Bear One Another’s Burdens
lessons.hear:
In a single passage, Paul says two things that seem to contradict each other: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2), and “For each man will bear his own burden” (Galatians 6:5). So which is it—carry each other’s, or carry your own?

In English both verses say “burden,” but Paul uses two different Greek words. The burden in verse 2 is a load too heavy for one person, like a boulder it takes several people to lift: a sudden illness, a lost job, the death of a loved one, a storm in a marriage, the shame that follows a fall. The burden in verse 5 is more like the pack each soldier carries on the march—the responsibility each of us bears before God.

A healthy church needs both. If everyone only carries their own, the church becomes a crowd of people each hauling a boulder and silently collapsing. If we only talk about carrying each other’s, it easily turns into some people depending on others forever while others over-carry until they burn out. The wisdom of love is this: lift the boulders together, carry your own backpack, and walk side by side all the way.

Paul especially mentions one kind of burden—sin. “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted” (Galatians 6:1). What a fallen member needs most isn’t onlookers and gossip, but a gentle pair of hands to help them up.

Why do this? Because “so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). Christ himself bore our heaviest burden—the penalty for sin. People who have been carried by him naturally bend down to pick up a brother’s burden.
lessons.light: When self-centered people see someone else’s burden, their first thought is “That’s not my problem,” or “Well, they should have been more careful.” Selfless people think, “The Lord once carried me like this.” Restoring with gentleness rather than condemning is a sign that Jesus reigns. At the same time, we keep watch over ourselves, because humble people know they could fall too.
think: In Galatians 6:1-5, what is the difference between the burden of verse 2 and the burden of verse 5?
At church, am I more likely to stand by indifferently, or to take on too much?
Who around me is carrying a boulder that needs others to help lift it?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for carrying my heaviest burden. Give me a heart willing to bend down, to see the boulders my fellow members can’t lift and to lift them together. Give me wisdom not to carry the backpack someone should carry themselves, but to walk beside them. When I meet someone who has fallen, help me restore them gently, not condemn them with words. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask a member who is going through a hard time, “During this season, is there one specific thing I can help you carry?” Then do it this week.
lessons.quick: Lift the boulders together, carry your own backpack, and walk side by side.
text: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.
But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.
For each man will bear his own burden.

lessons.title: Accepting Isn’t Being the Same
lessons.hear:
A Chinese church had two services. The morning service was mainly in Chinese and mostly attended by older members; the afternoon service was mainly in English and mostly attended by young people. Each had its own songs, fellowships, and lunches. Under one roof, they felt like two churches. At one combined Sunday service, the older members found the drums too loud and the younger ones found the hymns too slow. As people left, many thought, “We’re better off apart.”

This is a very common old mindset: unity means everyone being the same; if I’m going to accept someone, it would be best if they became like me first. But the church in Rome had Jews and Gentiles, those who ate only vegetables and those who ate everything, those who kept special days and those who didn’t—differences far bigger than our worship-style debates. Paul didn’t tell them to become the same. He said, “Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God” (Romans 15:7).

Think about it: when Christ accepted us, how different were we from him? He is holy; we were unclean. He is Lord; we were sinners. He didn’t require us to become good before he accepted us. He accepted us first, and then changed us. Paul says, “For even Christ didn’t please himself” (Romans 15:3), and quotes the Psalms: the reproaches of those who reproached God fell on him (see Psalm 69:9).

Paul’s hope is that “with one accord you may with one mouth glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 15:6). One mouth—not one vocal part. It’s like a choir: sopranos and basses each sing their own line, but it’s the same song under the same conductor. The psalmist marveled long ago: “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1).

Later, that church tried having the older members teach the young people an old hymn, and the young people teach the older members a new song. One elderly deacon smiled and said, “So your drums are worshiping God too.”
lessons.light: Self-centered acceptance has conditions: I’ll accept you if you’re like me. Selfless acceptance is Christlike: Christ accepted me, so I accept you. Pride makes my own tastes the standard; humility returns to its proper place and admits that only God is the standard. Accepting people who are different is exactly how we let Jesus receive all the glory.
think: In Romans 15:1-7, what does Paul give us as the model for accepting one another?
Do I expect others to become like me before I’m willing to accept them?
To which member of a different generation or culture can I reach out?
lessons.speak: Father, forgive me for so often accepting only people who are like me, and measuring your house by my own tastes. Thank you for accepting me when I was still so unlike you. Enlarge my heart to accept brothers and sisters of different generations, cultures, and backgrounds, so that with one accord and one mouth we may glorify you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, get to know a member of a different generation or cultural background. Ask them, “What’s your favorite worship song, and why?” and listen carefully.
lessons.quick: Unity isn’t sameness; it’s different people glorifying God with one mouth.
text: Now we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
Let each one of us please his neighbor for that which is good, to be building him up.
For even Christ didn’t please himself. But, as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.”
For whatever things were written before were written for our learning, that through perseverance and through encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.
Now the God of perseverance and of encouragement grant you to be of the same mind with one another according to Christ Jesus,
that with one accord you may with one mouth glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore accept one another, even as Christ also accepted you, to the glory of God.

lessons.title: No Disputes over Opinions
lessons.hear:
Around election time, church group chats are often at their quietest—and their tensest. One brother reposts a political commentary; a sister immediately replies with a long rebuttal; then someone quietly leaves the group. On Sunday everyone still smiles and says hello, but an invisible wall has gone up between them.

In Chinese churches everywhere, members hold different political positions, social views, and life experiences. The church in Rome had similar tensions, though the issues then were what to eat and whether to keep certain days. Paul begins, “Now accept one who is weak in faith, but not for disputes over opinions” (Romans 14:1).

This doesn’t mean nothing matters. Some things the Bible teaches clearly, and they touch the core of the gospel. But there are many other matters on which Christians who love the Lord just as much, and read the Bible just as faithfully, reach different judgments in different situations. For these, Paul gives an important reason: “Don’t let him who eats despise him who doesn’t eat. Don’t let him who doesn’t eat judge him who eats, for God has accepted him” (Romans 14:3). The brother who votes differently from you—God has already accepted him.

Then Paul lifts our eyes higher: “For if we live, we live to the Lord” (Romans 14:8). Our deepest identity isn’t membership in some camp; it is belonging to the Lord.

Here is how to practice today. 1. Don’t forward aggressive political or divisive messages in church group chats. 2. When you want to understand a member who sees things differently, ask, “Why does this matter so much to you?” rather than “How could you possibly think that?” 3. Pray together with them for your city and your nation. When we kneel together, we discover we are standing before the same Lord.
lessons.light: From a worldly perspective to God’s perspective: earthly positions are temporary; our identity in the Lord is eternal. Self-centered people want others to stand on my side; selfless people stand with their brothers on the Lord’s side. People matter more than issues—don’t lose a brother to win an argument.
think: In Romans 14:1-8, how does Paul handle differing views among believers?
Have I ever distanced myself in my heart from a member because of a different position?
How can I pray together with a member whose views differ from mine?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the King of kings, and the Lord of each one of us. Forgive me for valuing my own position more than my brother, and building walls in my heart. Remind me that you have already accepted the member who sees things differently from me. Teach me to argue less and listen more, and to pray with them before you for our city. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, review what you’ve been posting in church group chats, and stop forwarding aggressive or divisive messages. Then message a member whose views differ from yours and invite them to pray together for your city.
lessons.quick: God has accepted them; I won’t dispute opinions but will accept them.
text: Now accept one who is weak in faith, but not for disputes over opinions.
One man has faith to eat all things, but he who is weak eats only vegetables.
Don’t let him who eats despise him who doesn’t eat. Don’t let him who doesn’t eat judge him who eats, for God has accepted him.
Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.
One man esteems one day as more important. Another esteems every day alike. Let each man be fully assured in his own mind.

He who observes the day, observes it to the Lord; and he who does not observe the day, to the Lord he does not observe it. He who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives God thanks. He who doesn’t eat, to the Lord he doesn’t eat, and gives God thanks.
For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself.
For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.

lessons.title: Jonah and His Exception List
lessons.hear:
Jonah was a very unusual prophet. His message brought an entire city to repentance, yet he himself was deeply unhappy. Nineveh was the great city of Assyria, Israel’s enemy, notorious for its brutality. When God spared them, Jonah prayed angrily, “for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness” (Jonah 4:2). His theology was perfectly correct; his heart was shut tight.

So he went out of the city, built a shelter, and sat waiting to see what would happen to it. God provided a vine to shade him, and he was overjoyed. Then God sent a worm that killed the vine, and Jonah was so angry he wanted to die. God said to him, “You have been concerned for the vine, for which you have not labored, neither made it grow; which came up in a night, and perished in a night. Shouldn’t I be concerned for Nineveh, that great city … ?” (Jonah 4:10-11).

The book of Jonah ends on that question. It never tells us how Jonah answered. Perhaps the question is left for every reader.

Examine yourself honestly: Who is the Nineveh in my heart? Maybe it’s people from another generation, an ethnic group I was taught from childhood to be wary of, people on the opposite side of politics, or the kind of people who once hurt my family. Like Jonah, I may sing in church that God’s love is unconditional while keeping a list in my heart of “everyone except these people.” Paul’s question is just as direct: “But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you again, why do you despise your brother?” (Romans 14:10).

Accepting someone doesn’t mean approving of everything they do, nor denying past wounds. It means acknowledging that God cares for them as he cares for me. The adjustment starts small: bring your exception list before God, and let his question echo in your heart: “Is it right for you to be angry?” (Jonah 4:4).
lessons.light: Jonah’s problem wasn’t in his head but in his heart. He knew God’s grace, yet wanted to decide who could receive it—that is the self-centered life: leaving our proper place as human beings and trying to take God’s place. Humility lets God be God: whomever he cares for, I follow him in caring for.
think: In Jonah 4:5-11, how does God speak to Jonah?
Do I have a list in my heart of “everyone except these people”?
For which person or group on that list am I willing to start praying?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that sometimes I’m like Jonah: my mouth says you are gracious and merciful, but my heart doesn’t want your grace to reach certain people. Search me and tear up my exception list. Help me care for those you care for, and accept the brothers and sisters you have already accepted. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the group of people you find hardest to accept. Pray for one person or one family among them, asking God to bless them, and keep praying for them for seven days in a row.
lessons.quick: Whom God cares for, I learn to care for; hand your exception list to the Lord.
text: Then Jonah went out of the city and sat on the east side of the city, and there made himself a booth and sat under it in the shade, until he might see what would become of the city.
The LORD God prepared a vine and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head to deliver him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the vine.
But God prepared a worm at dawn the next day, and it chewed on the vine so that it withered.

When the sun arose, God prepared a sultry east wind; and the sun beat on Jonah’s head, so that he was faint and requested for himself that he might die. He said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”
God said to Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the vine?” He said, “I am right to be angry, even to death.”
The LORD said, “You have been concerned for the vine, for which you have not labored, neither made it grow; which came up in a night and perished in a night.

Shouldn’t I be concerned for Nineveh, that great city, in which are more than one hundred twenty thousand persons who can’t discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also many animals?”

lessons.title: The Great Choir Before the Throne
lessons.hear:
In his vision John saw an astonishing scene: “a great multitude, which no man could count, out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9). Their skin colors, languages, and histories were different, yet they wore the same white robes and cried out with one voice: “Salvation be to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:10).

This is the church’s future, and the church today is a rehearsal for that eternal choir. The older member from another generation you welcomed in your small group, the family who just moved here from far away, the brother whose politics differ from yours, the sister who just fell and is being helped back up—one day all of them will stand with you before the same throne. Since we will worship together in heaven forever, let’s start learning on earth today to bear with and accept one another.

This week we learned to lift the boulders together and carry our own backpacks; that accepting isn’t being the same; not to dispute over opinions; and to hand the exception list in our hearts to God. None of these lessons is learned once and for all. Bearing others’ burdens is tiring, and accepting people who are different is uncomfortable. That is why Paul encourages us: “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season if we don’t give up” (Galatians 6:9).

The way to multiply is concrete: let your small group become a rehearsal space for the throne room. At your next meeting, invite someone who is a little different from everyone else. Or set aside a time for burden-bearing, where one member shares their burden and the group takes on practical tasks to help. And teach what you’ve received this week to your children or a young person: in God’s house, people who are different are all our family.

When the church lives this way, the world will see on earth a preview of heaven.
lessons.light: From earth to heaven, from temporary to eternal: the people I accept today are the ones who will stand with me before the throne. Letting Jesus receive all the glory means people of every nation, tribe, and people finding a home among us. This is the pattern for building God’s system—may God’s kingdom come, on earth as it is in heaven.
think: In Revelation 7:9-12, what marks the multitude worshiping before the throne?
This week, what was my biggest breakthrough or struggle in bearing with or accepting others?
Which “different” person will I invite into my small group or my life?
lessons.speak: O Lamb of God, with your blood you purchased us for God from every nation, tribe, people, and language. Make our church a rehearsal for the worship before your throne, starting today: bearing one another’s burdens and accepting one another’s differences. Help me not grow weary in doing good, and help me pass this acceptance on to the next generation. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a member whose background differs from your small group’s to join a meeting or share a meal. Also suggest setting aside five minutes in small group for bearing burdens, where members take on specific ways to help one another.
lessons.quick: Those we accept today are the family who will stand with us before the throne.
text: After these things I looked, and behold, a great multitude which no man could count, out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, dressed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands.
They cried with a loud voice, saying, “Salvation be to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!”
All the angels were standing around the throne, the elders, and the four living creatures; and they fell on their faces before his throne, and worshiped God,
saying, “Amen! Blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, and might, be to our God forever and ever! Amen.”

weeks.title: Forgiving and Bearing with One Another
weeks.keyText: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
weeks.theme: I can forgive because I was forgiven first; I can bear with others because the Lord is still bearing with me.
group: Read Colossians 3:12-15. What attitudes does Paul tell us to put on, and what are the basis and the measure of our forgiveness?
How does the statement “Forgiveness doesn’t mean denying the hurt, and it doesn’t mean instantly restoring trust” help or challenge you?
This week, who is one person who hurt you that you are willing to pray for, or one person you have wronged to whom you could say, “I’m sorry”?
weeks.sunday: As you worship this Lord’s Day, deliberately remember how the Lord has forgiven you. If there is a name that still stings, don’t pretend everything is fine; place that person in the Lord’s hands and say quietly, “Lord, I’m willing to begin.” During the service, remember that this brother or sister is also someone who has received grace. Afterward, give a nod and a greeting to someone you’ve had friction with, or silently pray a sentence of blessing over them.

lessons.title: Putting On the Clothes of Forgiveness
lessons.hear:
In Colossians 3, Paul uses a very everyday picture: changing clothes. Just before this he tells us to take off the old self; here he tells us what to put on: “Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance” (Colossians 3:12). Notice the order—identity first, then behavior. You don’t forgive in order to become beloved; you are able to forgive because you are already beloved.

Then Paul gets very practical: “bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any” (Colossians 3:13). He doesn’t assume the church will be free of complaints. Whenever real people live together, there will be collisions: a careless remark, a ministry effort nobody noticed, a promise that was never kept. God’s family is not a place without friction; it is a place where friction can be handled by grace.

There are two verbs here. “Bearing with” deals with everyday imperfection: someone’s personality, habits, or way of doing things rubs me the wrong way, but it isn’t necessarily sin, so I carry it in love. “Forgiving” deals with real wrongs: the other person really was in the wrong and really did hurt me, yet I choose not to make them pay. Neither one means pretending nothing happened. Both mean I have seen it and named it, but I refuse to let it rule me.

What is the measure of forgiveness? “Even as Christ forgave you, so you also do” (Colossians 3:13). The source is not the size of my heart but the cross. Finally Paul says, “Let the peace of God rule in your hearts” (Colossians 3:15)—and the word “rule” originally meant to act as an umpire. Let God’s peace blow the whistle and make the call, rather than letting my sense of grievance hand down the verdict.
lessons.light: Self-centered people keep accounts, because “I” am at the center and they remember exactly who owes them what. Selfless people cancel accounts, because their focus is on Jesus—He has already canceled a far greater debt for me. Letting God’s peace rule in my heart is how I let Jesus reign: my grievance is not the judge; His cross hands down the verdict.
think: In Colossians 3:12-15, what attitudes does Paul tell us to put on, and what is the measure of forgiveness?
Is there something at church that I act as if I’m over, while inside I’m still keeping score?
Which brother or sister can I bear with today, and in what particular imperfection?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank You for forgiving me first and carrying all my debts on the cross. I confess that I am still hiding some accounts in my heart; sometimes I pretend all is well, and sometimes I quietly hold a grudge. Let Your peace rule in my heart, and clothe me with compassion, kindness, and patience, so that I forgive others just as You have forgiven me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, take five quiet minutes and write at the top of a page, “Debts the Lord has canceled for me,” then list three. Below that, write the name of one brother or sister you need to bear with, and write one sentence of blessing for them.
lessons.quick: I can forgive because the Lord forgave me first.
text: Put on therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, a heart of compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance;
bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.
Above all these things, walk in love, which is the bond of perfection.
And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body, and be thankful.

lessons.title: Ten Thousand Talents and a Hundred Denarii
lessons.hear:
A sister who had sung in the choir for years was once publicly accused of being “uncooperative” by another ministry team member during a team meeting. She went home and cried all night. From then on, every time she saw that person at rehearsal, her stomach knotted up. She thought, “He has never apologized. Why should I forgive him?”

This is an old mindset we know well: forgiveness is a reward, handed out only after the other person admits fault and behaves well enough. Forgiveness also has a limit, and once it is used up, we can stop. Peter thought the same way, so he asked the Lord, “Until seven times?” (Matthew 18:21). But Jesus said, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22). He wasn’t telling us to count to four hundred ninety; He was telling us to stop counting.

Then the Lord told a parable. A servant owed the king ten thousand talents—a debt he could never repay in a lifetime. Yet the king, “being moved with compassion, released him, and forgave him the debt” (Matthew 18:27). The moment that same servant walked out, he ran into a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii, and he grabbed him by the throat. The absurdity of the story is a portrait of us: every day we live in the grace of ten thousand talents forgiven, yet we grab a brother by the throat over a hundred denarii.

Notice that Jesus never says the hundred denarii weren’t a real debt. The fellow servant truly owed it; the hurt is real. God’s perspective doesn’t ask us to say, “It’s nothing.” It asks us to set this real debt beside the ten thousand talents of grace and weigh it again. Forgiveness is not a reward but a response. We forgive not because the other person deserves it, but because we didn’t deserve it either, and yet we received grace.

Later that sister prayed, “Lord, what he owes me is real, but what You have forgiven me is far more. I hand this account over to You.” Her stomach didn’t unclench right away, but she knew her hands had let go.
lessons.light: Those who refuse to forgive think they are punishing the other person, but they are really locking themselves in prison. The self-centered life sees only “he owes me”; the selfless life first sees “I owe the Lord.” Shift from man’s perspective to God’s: the other person’s hundred denarii are real, and the ten thousand talents the Lord forgave me are even more real.
think: How much was the servant in the parable forgiven, and how did he then treat his fellow servant?
Do I carry a list of conditions in my heart, such as “I’ll forgive once they apologize first”?
Of the ten thousand talents the Lord has forgiven me, which debt am I most grateful for today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often treat forgiveness as a reward, holding it back until the other person behaves well enough. Today I stand before You and see that I owed You ten thousand talents, and You forgave it all. Help me to forgive from my heart—not by denying the hurt, but by placing this real debt into Your hands. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, draw two columns on a sheet of paper: “A Hundred Denarii” and “Ten Thousand Talents.” In the left column, write what a brother or sister owes you; in the right, write what the Lord has forgiven you. After you pray, draw a cross over the left column.
lessons.quick: Their hundred denarii are real; the ten thousand talents the Lord forgave me are even more real.
text: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.
Therefore the Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants.
When he had begun to settle, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents.
But because he couldn’t pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, with his wife, his children, and all that he had, and payment to be made.
The servant therefore fell down and knelt before him, saying, ‘Lord, have patience with me, and I will repay you all!’
The lord of that servant, being moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the debt.
“But that servant went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him one hundred denarii, and he grabbed him and took him by the throat, saying, ‘Pay me what you owe!’
“So his fellow servant fell down at his feet and begged him, saying, ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you!’
He would not, but went and cast him into prison until he should pay back that which was due.
So when his fellow servants saw what was done, they were exceedingly sorry, and came and told their lord all that was done.
Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.
Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’
His lord was angry, and delivered him to the tormentors until he should pay all that was due to him.
So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds.”

lessons.title: A Prayer of Forgiveness, Starting Today
lessons.hear:
There is a line in the Lord’s Prayer that we have said countless times, often too quickly: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). The Lord puts being forgiven and forgiving others into the same sentence, as if to say that no one can hold out one hand to receive grace while clenching the other into a fist. This doesn’t mean we earn salvation by forgiving others. It means that a heart that has truly been forgiven will always let forgiveness flow out. If nothing flows at all, we need to go back and ask whether we have really understood grace.

Forgiveness is usually not a single event finished in an instant; it is a process that begins with a decision. Today you can practice three steps in prayer:
First, tell the truth: before the Lord, say specifically, “This is what they did, and this is how much it hurt.” Forgiveness doesn’t deny the hurt; you don’t have to pretend it doesn’t hurt.
Second, give up the right to collect: tell the Lord, “I will no longer chase this debt myself; I hand it to You.” Vengeance and repayment belong to God (see Romans 12:19). What you lay down is not justice, but your seat as the judge.
Third, bless them: even if it is only, “Lord, please take care of them too.” It may feel forced at first, and that’s all right. Feelings often follow obedience.

Remember, too, that forgiveness does not mean immediately restoring the trust you once had. You can forgive a ministry partner who hurt you from the heart, and still, for now, not serve alone with them. Trust has to be rebuilt through the other person’s repentance and over time. If the harm involves abuse of power, violence, or violation, then forgiveness certainly doesn’t mean staying silent. Seeking help from trustworthy elders and deacons, a supervising church body, or professional help is biblical protection, not unforgiveness.
lessons.light: Letting Jesus reign includes letting Him sit on the judgment seat. Clinging to the right to repay is leaving our proper place and trying to take God’s place; handing the account to the Lord is returning to our proper place. Forgiveness is an act of humility: I am not the judge; I am a sinner who has received grace.
think: In Matthew 6:12-15, how does the Lord tie being forgiven to forgiving others?
Is there someone I have been quietly judging in God’s place?
For which brother or sister will I pray today using these three steps?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I bring that name in my heart before You. The way they hurt me is real, and it hurts deeply—You know it all. Today I decide not to chase this debt myself. I hand it over to You, and I ask You to bless them. My feelings haven’t caught up yet, so I ask the Holy Spirit to keep working in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Find a quiet time today and use the three steps—tell the truth, give up the right to collect, bless them—to pray for a brother or sister who hurt you. Write the date in your journal as the starting point of your forgiveness.
lessons.quick: Forgiveness begins with a decision: I hand this debt to the Lord.
text: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’
“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.
But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.

lessons.title: Pulling Up the Root of Bitterness
lessons.hear:
Some hurts happened long ago, and we assume we’re over them. Yet the moment we hear that person’s name or see them leading worship up front, something sour rises inside. Paul gives a string of words: “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31). The list looks a lot like a tree. Bitterness is the root buried underground; wrath is the resentment simmering inside; anger and outcry are the branches breaking above the surface; slander and malice are the fruit. Hebrews warns us as well: “lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and many be defiled by it” (Hebrews 12:15). Bitterness is never just a private matter.

Today, review honestly. Don’t review how wrong the other person was; review what has grown in your own heart. Do I keep replaying that scene in my mind? In my small group or at home, do I—intentionally or not—let people know “what kind of person he really is”? Do I secretly hope she’ll slip up where everyone can see? These are all signs that the root is still there.

The direction for adjustment is in the next verse: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). The key is the phrase “just as.” The power to change doesn’t come from gritting our teeth but from returning to the source. Peter denied the Lord three times, yet the risen Lord prepared a charcoal fire and breakfast for him by the sea, asked him three times whether he loved Him, and restored his calling (see John 21:15-17). A man forgiven like that later urged believers not to repay evil for evil, but to bless instead (see 1 Peter 3:9).

Pulling up a root takes time, and sometimes more than one attempt. But every time you bring your bitterness to the cross, the root loosens a little more.
lessons.light: Bitterness is the most stubborn root of the self-centered life: I was hurt, so I have the right not to let go. Being selfless doesn’t mean feeling nothing; it means not letting the wound reign. This is where the “0” of 920 is practiced—seeing even the brother or sister who makes my heart ache as one of the “2” the Lord wants me to love.
think: What does Ephesians 4:31 tell us to put away? What does “just as” in Ephesians 4:32 point to?
Whose name makes the sourness of bitterness rise in my heart?
How will I stop describing that person to others?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, shine Your light on the bitterness hidden in my heart. I often replay my wounds, and I quietly slander others in front of people. Forgive me, pull up this poisonous root, and make me kind and tenderhearted. Just as God in Christ forgave me, enable me to forgive in the same way. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, whenever you feel the urge to talk about the brother or sister who hurt you, turn it into a silent one-sentence prayer for them instead. If the wound is too deep, share it with a mature, trustworthy companion and ask them to pray for you—that is seeking help, not slander.
lessons.quick: Bitterness is a root and forgiveness pulls it up; every return to the cross loosens it a little more.
text: Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.title: Am I in the Place of God?
lessons.hear:
Joseph’s story is the most moving—and most honest—story of forgiveness in the Old Testament. His brothers sold him into Egypt. That was no misunderstanding; it was deliberate evil. Years later, when he had become ruler over Egypt and his brothers came to buy grain, he didn’t reveal himself right away. Instead he tested them again and again to see whether they had changed. Only when Judah offered to become a slave in Benjamin’s place (see Genesis 44:33) did Joseph weep aloud and tell them who he was. Forgiveness may have begun in his heart long before, but the relationship and trust were restored only after he saw genuine repentance.

After their father died, the brothers were afraid again. Joseph’s answer carries great weight: “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?” (Genesis 50:19). He would not sit in the judge’s seat. Then he said, “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). He didn’t say, “You didn’t hurt me.” He called it evil plainly. Forgiveness doesn’t deny the harm, but it sees that God is bigger than the harm.

This week we have learned: we forgive because we were forgiven first; bearing with one another means carrying each other’s imperfections in love; forgiveness doesn’t mean denying the hurt, and it doesn’t mean instantly restoring trust; and bitterness must be brought to the cross again and again to be uprooted. Joseph lived out every one of these.
