Multiplication means letting forgiveness keep flowing to those around you. Your children, your small group members, and friends who are new in the faith are all watching how you handle hurt. When they see that you don’t retaliate, don’t give people the silent treatment, and don’t pretend nothing happened—but instead honestly entrust it to God, gently keep healthy boundaries, and keep on blessing—they learn a lesson deeper than any teaching.
lessons.light: Pride grasps God’s power and even wants to handle repayment itself; humility returns to our proper place: “Am I in the place of God?” (Genesis 50:19). Joseph let God be God and himself be a man, and the result was the preservation of his whole family. Change begins with me, forgiveness begins with me, and it is passed on to the next generation at home and in the church.
think: How did Joseph describe what his brothers had done, and how did he view what God had done?
Is it easier for me to deny the hurt, or harder for me to give up judging?
With whom will I share what I’ve learned about forgiveness this week?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You for teaching me to forgive this week. I don’t have to pretend I wasn’t hurt, and I don’t have to sit in the judgment seat, because You are a God who is both just and loving. Like Joseph, help me see that You are bigger than the harm, and let forgiveness flow from me into my home and my small group. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This weekend, meet with a spiritual companion or a small group member and share what “Forgiveness doesn’t mean denying the hurt, and it doesn’t mean instantly restoring trust” means to you. Then pray for each other about a relationship that needs forgiveness.
lessons.quick: Am I in the place of God? I let God be God, and I learn to forgive.
text: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.”
They sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father commanded before he died, saying,

‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.”
Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.
Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.

weeks.title: Welcoming and Serving One Another
weeks.keyText: Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
weeks.theme: Open the door and reach out your hands; the grace I have received is meant to flow on to others.
group: Read 1 Peter 4:7-11. Why, right after saying “the end of all things is near,” does Peter specifically call us to hospitality and service?
What most often keeps you from welcoming or serving others—circumstances, time, personality, or grumbling in your heart?
This week, which brother or sister or new friend are you willing to invite for a meal or a cup of tea? How could your small group do this together?
weeks.sunday: This Lord’s Day, arrive a little early and think of yourself as a host in this family, not a guest. During the service, watch for someone sitting alone or visiting for the first time. Afterward, go and sit beside them, ask their name, and invite them to share a meal or a cup of tea. Before you head home, thank the Lord for them and for the gifts He has given you.

lessons.title: Doors Open, Hands Outstretched
lessons.hear:
When Peter wrote these words, believers were facing persecution and scattered far from home. Normally, in hard times people shut their doors and guard what they have. Yet Peter says, “The end of all things is near” (1 Peter 4:7), so be sober in prayer and love one another earnestly—and then comes a very down-to-earth instruction: “Be hospitable to one another without grumbling” (1 Peter 4:9). Seeing life in light of the end doesn’t make us hoard; it makes us open our doors.

In the New Testament, the word for “hospitality” literally means “love of strangers.” In an age without hotel chains, traveling preachers, brothers fleeing danger, and sisters arriving from distant towns all depended on believers’ homes for a place to stay. The early church had no grand buildings; the gospel spread from one open living room and dinner table to the next.

Then Peter says, “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms” (1 Peter 4:10). “Various forms” carries the sense of something richly many-colored, like a single beam of light split by a prism into a spectrum. Some are gifted in words, others in deeds. One person can cook a whole feast, another can fix a leaky pipe, and another is wonderful at keeping an elderly saint company. No color is superfluous, and no one comes empty-handed.

Notice the word “managers”—stewards. Gifts are not my property; they are what the Master has entrusted to my care. A steward succeeds not by looking impressive, but by making sure the Master’s goods reach the people they were meant for. That is why Peter concludes, “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 4:11). In the end, hospitality and service are not about proving how welcoming or capable I am. They are about letting people meet, at our table and through our hands, the Lord who welcomed us first.
lessons.light: Let Jesus receive all the glory: if I serve so people will notice me, it becomes a performance; if I serve so people will see Jesus, I am a steward. The gifts are God’s and I am His steward—this is returning to my proper place. Denying myself means living for Jesus and for others, not for myself, and handing my front door and my two hands over to the Lord’s use.
think: In 1 Peter 4:7-11, in light of what kind of times does Peter place hospitality and service?
Do I treat my gifts as my own property, or as a stewardship entrusted to me by the Lord?
What “color” of grace is in my hands that could flow to others this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank You for welcoming me first; at Your table, this stranger became family. Help me stop keeping the door of my home and the door of my heart shut, and make me willing to be hospitable without grumbling. Everything I have is entrusted to me by You. Use my hands, so that in all things You may be glorified. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, list three things you have that could serve others—such as a favorite dish you make, a skill, or a block of free time. Next to each, write the name of a brother or sister who might need it.
lessons.quick: My gifts are not my property; they are grace meant to flow out.
text: But the end of all things is near. Therefore be of sound mind, self-controlled, and sober in prayer.
And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.
Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

lessons.title: Running from the Tent Door
lessons.hear:
A young couple living in a tiny apartment never dared to invite their small group over. They thought, “The living room is too small, we don’t have enough bowls, and I can’t really cook. We’ll do it once we move somewhere bigger.” Then one day a brother who had recently moved to the city for work fell ill. They couldn’t bear to leave him alone, so they made a pot of rice porridge with a few simple side dishes and invited him over. Halfway through the meal, his eyes filled with tears: “I’ve been in this city for six months, and this is the first time anyone has invited me into their home.”

We often carry an old mindset: hospitality means hosting a dinner party. You need a presentable home and cooking you can be proud of, and you need to be outgoing and good with guests. If it can’t be perfect, better not to start. But that turns hospitality into a performance. The focus becomes “Is my home good enough?” instead of “Does this person have a need?”

Look at Abraham. It was the heat of the day, and he was sitting at his tent door when he saw three strangers. “He ran to meet them from the tent door” (Genesis 18:2). He was ninety-nine years old, and he was still running. He invited them to wash their feet and rest, offering only “a piece of bread,” but he actually served cakes of fine meal, a tender calf, butter, and milk. The most moving detail is the last line: “He stood by them under the tree, and they ate” (Genesis 18:8). The host didn’t take the seat of honor and hold court; he stood nearby, attentive to whatever his guests needed.

Looking back on this scene, the book of Hebrews says, “Don’t forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2). God’s perspective is that hospitality isn’t about showing off my home; it’s about letting people find rest in it. When you open your door, you may be welcoming the Lord Himself. In God’s eyes, a pot of porridge can be a banquet.
lessons.light: Self-centered hospitality asks, “What will people think of me?” Selfless hospitality asks, “What does this person need?” Abraham standing by to serve is a picture of returning to a servant’s proper place. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The size of the house and the quality of the food are things; the person you welcome through the door is what matters.
think: In welcoming his guests, what actions reveal Abraham’s heart?
Have I, too, kept my door shut because things aren’t “perfect enough”?
What is the simplest way I can begin showing hospitality to one person?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often treat hospitality as a performance. Afraid my home isn’t nice enough or that I’m not a good enough host, I shut the door. Give me Abraham’s running heart, so that I care more about people’s needs than about saving face. Let my small home also become a place where people find rest. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of a brother or sister who lives alone, has moved from elsewhere, or is new to the church. Send them a message inviting them to a simple meal this week at your home or a nearby café. The place and the menu don’t have to be perfect.
lessons.quick: Hospitality isn’t showing off my home; it’s letting people find rest there.
text: The LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day.
He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood near him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth,
and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant.
Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
I will get a piece of bread so you can refresh your heart. After that you may go your way, now that you have come to your servant.” They said, “Very well, do as you have said.”
Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah, and said, “Quickly prepare three seahs of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes.”
Abraham ran to the herd, and fetched a tender and good calf, and gave it to the servant. He hurried to dress it.
He took butter, milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree, and they ate.

lessons.title: One More Pair of Chopsticks
lessons.hear:
Chinese families have a warm habit: when someone drops by, you simply set out one more pair of chopsticks. You don’t need a separate table; you just share a portion of what is already there. Paul’s instruction to the church in Romans is much the same: “contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality.” (Romans 12:13). The word behind “given to” carries the idea of pursuing, of going after something with energy. It isn’t waiting for guests to show up at the door; it is actively seeking out people to welcome.

This verse also comes at the end of a whole series of descriptions of love: “Let love be without hypocrisy,” and “In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another” (Romans 12:9-10). Clearly, hospitality is not a set of hosting techniques. It is love finding a dinner table.

Today’s practice is to set out one more pair of chopsticks. Here is how you can start:
First, choose someone: watch for those who are easily overlooked—first-time visitors, seniors who live alone, students or migrant workers far from home, families who have recently lost a loved one or a job.
Second, start simple: a bowl of noodles, a pot of tea, or a boxed lunch together after the Sunday service is plenty. For those in online gatherings, you can stay on ten extra minutes after the meeting ends to keep a new friend company one-on-one.
Third, bring your heart, not a show: ask a good question or two, listen quietly, and pray for them at the end. More than the food, people remember being seen and heard.

“Contributing to the needs of the saints” also reminds us that hospitality sometimes looks like a bag of rice, going along to a doctor’s appointment, or helping someone move. Service isn’t always on the platform; more often it happens in someone else’s kitchen, at a hospital bedside, or among moving boxes. When you live this way, you are helping the church become a family, not just a meeting.
lessons.light: Use your heart and rely on the Holy Spirit, not your head and yourself. Head-driven hospitality counts the cost and worries about what people will think, and the more you think, the more anxious you get. Heart-driven hospitality simply asks the Holy Spirit, “Who would You like me to set out an extra pair of chopsticks for today?” 920 starts with the “2” closest to you, and a single meal can turn a member of the congregation into family.
think: In Romans 12:9-13, what expressions of love are linked with hospitality?
Which kind of people in my church do I most often overlook?
Who will I set out “one more pair of chopsticks” for this week, and when and where?
lessons.speak: Lord, at Your table there has always been a seat for me. Open my eyes to see the brothers and sisters around me who are in need or lonely, and give me a heart that welcomes others actively—without keeping score and without putting on a show. May my table, my time, and my hands become an extension of Your love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a brother or sister who is easily overlooked to share a meal with you. During the meal, ask them two caring questions, listen quietly, and pray for them before you part.
lessons.quick: One more pair of chopsticks, and the church gains one more family member.
text: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor that which is evil. Cling to that which is good.
In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor prefer one another,
not lagging in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord,
rejoicing in hope, enduring in troubles, continuing steadfastly in prayer,
contributing to the needs of the saints, and given to hospitality.

lessons.title: Martha’s Distraction
lessons.hear:
Martha was a warmly hospitable woman. When Jesus came to the village, she was the one who “received him into her house” (Luke 10:38). Her mistake wasn’t serving; the problem was that something else grew up in the middle of her serving: “Martha was distracted with much serving” (Luke 10:40). Then she went to Jesus to complain about her sister, and even blamed Jesus Himself: “Lord, don’t you care?”

This scene plays out in churches every day. In the kitchen after a fellowship meal, someone always sighs while washing dishes: “It’s always the same few of us doing everything.” A children’s ministry worker serves for a whole year, no one says thank you, and her heart grows more and more sour. Once service drifts away from Jesus’ feet, it turns from love into a burden, and then from a burden into grumbling. Peter specifically said “be hospitable to one another without grumbling” because he knew that grumbling is the most common poison in service.

Today, honestly review a few questions. Do I need to be noticed in order to have the energy to serve? Do I often compare who is doing more and who is doing less? Am I so busy that I have no time to sit at the Lord’s feet? Jesus said gently, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed” (Luke 10:41-42). The Lord said her name twice—not to scold her, but because His heart went out to her.

The comforting thing is that Martha changed. When Lazarus died, she made a profound confession of faith to the Lord: “Yes, Lord. I have come to believe that you are the Christ, God’s Son” (John 11:27). Later, when a dinner was prepared for Jesus, Scripture simply notes, “Martha served” (John 12:2). She was still serving, but this time there is no record of complaint. Adjustment doesn’t mean you stop serving; it means you first return to the Lord’s feet and go out from there.
lessons.light: Self-centered service revolves around me: how much I’ve done, who noticed, who did less than me. Selfless service revolves around Jesus: God first, then people, then tasks. When the order of those relationships gets jumbled, service becomes frantic; when we return to the Lord’s feet, service turns from a burden back into joy.
think: How did Jesus respond to Martha, and what problem did He point out?
Where in my service have comparison or grumbling already taken root?
This week, how will I sit at the Lord’s feet first before going out to serve?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I confess that I am often like Martha—busy serving but far from Your feet, comparing and complaining, even blaming You for not caring. Forgive me. Teach me to listen to Your word first, and then to serve with the strength You supply. May my service be free of grumbling and full of thanksgiving. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, before your next time of serving, spend ten quiet minutes reading Scripture and praying. Afterward, give a co-worker who served alongside you one specific word of thanks.
lessons.quick: Sit at the Lord’s feet first, and serving won’t turn into grumbling.
text: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.title: A Home Became a Church
lessons.hear:
When Paul first set foot in Europe, he met a group of women gathered for prayer by a river outside the city of Philippi. One of them was named Lydia, a businesswoman who dealt in purple cloth. Scripture says the Lord “opened” her heart (Acts 16:14). After she believed and was baptized, her very first response was to open her home: “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house, and stay” (Acts 16:15).

First the door of her heart was opened by the Lord; then the door of her home was opened to others. That is hospitality’s most natural order. Later, Paul and Silas were beaten and thrown into prison. Where did they go when they were released? “They went out of the prison, and entered into Lydia’s house. When they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them” (Acts 16:40). A home became the place where the church in Philippi gathered and found comfort, and that church went on to become one of Paul’s greatest sources of joy and one of his closest partners in the gospel (see Philippians 1:3-5).

This week we have seen that hospitality is love for strangers, and service is being a steward of God’s grace in its various forms. Abraham’s running tells us we don’t have to be perfect, only willing. Martha reminds us that service must flow from the Lord’s feet. Now let what we have received keep multiplying.

Multiplication can begin by bringing someone along. Next time you show hospitality, invite a younger brother or sister, or your own child, to prepare with you: washing vegetables together, setting the table, greeting the guests, and praying together after the meal. Many people learn hospitality not from hearing a sermon, but from once being loved at someone else’s table and learning to serve at someone else’s side. A door you open today may, years from now, become the starting point of another home, another small group, even another church.
lessons.light: The “3” of 235 is about building relationships of spiritual parents and children, and the best classroom is often a dinner table. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: the Lord first opened Lydia’s heart, then she opened her home, and finally her home became a base for ministry. Building God’s system often begins with an open living room.
think: What did Lydia do after she believed, and what did her home later become?
Which is still more tightly shut—the door of my heart or the door of my home?
Which younger brother or sister will I invite to learn hospitality with me?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You for opening my heart; now I ask You to open my home as well. Like Lydia’s home, may mine become a place where brothers and sisters are comforted and new friends meet You. Help me not only to serve myself, but to bring the next generation along to learn hospitality and service together. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This weekend, invite a younger brother or sister, or your child, to prepare a simple time of hospitality with you: shop for groceries together, set the table, welcome the guests, pray together for your guests after the meal, and share what you have learned this week.
lessons.quick: When the heart’s door opens to the Lord, the home’s door opens to people.
text: On the Sabbath day we went outside of the city by a riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together.
A certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, one who worshiped God, heard us. The Lord opened her heart to listen to the things which were spoken by Paul.
When she and her household were baptized, she begged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” So she persuaded us.

weeks.title: Encouraging and Building Up One Another
weeks.keyText: Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do.
weeks.theme: My words are not for tearing down but for building; today I will build someone up with a single sentence.
group: Read 1 Thessalonians 5:11-15. What different kinds of people does Paul mention, and what kind of words does each one need?
Has a particular sentence ever built you up—or cut you deeply? How did those words affect you afterward?
This week, each small group member chooses one brother or sister and gives them a specific word of encouragement. At the next meeting, share how they responded.
weeks.sunday: Before the service this Lord’s Day, ask the Lord for eyes that see grace. During the service, notice a brother or sister who serves quietly or looks weary. Afterward, go over and tell them specifically the grace you see in them—for example, “Thank you for greeting people at the door every week; you make me feel welcome”—and pray a sentence of blessing over them.

lessons.title: Building a House with Words
lessons.hear:
When Paul wrote to the church in Thessalonica, they had only recently come to faith, and already they faced persecution as well as grief over loved ones who had died. Paul didn’t simply tell them to grit their teeth. Instead he wrote, “Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do” (1 Thessalonians 5:11).

There are two vivid words here. “Exhort” originally means to come alongside someone and call out to them—like when you’re running a marathon and someone runs up beside you for a stretch, saying, “Hang in there, you can do this.” “Build up” comes from the language of constructing a house. Paul’s point is that the church is built not only by words from the pulpit but also by the everyday words of each member, sentence by sentence, brick by brick. On the other hand, one careless remark can knock down a wall that someone has worked hard to build.

Then Paul gets more specific: “Admonish the disorderly; encourage the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient toward all” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). Three kinds of people need three kinds of words. Those who are careless and undisciplined need an honest reminder. Those who are discouraged need a warm word to lift their spirits. Those who are weak need more than words—they need someone to reach out a hand and steady them. Encouragement is not a one-size-fits-all script. First see clearly where the person in front of you is, then say what they need to hear. That takes the Holy Spirit’s guidance, and it takes truly knowing one another.

Finally, notice the phrase “even as you also do.” Paul first affirms what they are already doing, then urges them to keep going. That itself is a model of encouragement: first see the grace, then point the way forward. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to make your mouth a tool for building.
lessons.light: Self-centered speech focuses on expressing me: my opinions, my complaints, whether I am right. Selfless speech focuses on building others up: will saying this draw the other person closer to Jesus? Letting the Holy Spirit be my guide includes letting Him govern my tongue.
think: In 1 Thessalonians 5:14, how should each of the three kinds of people be treated?
At church, are my words more often building up or tearing down?
Which brother or sister near me is discouraged or weak right now and needs me to run alongside them for a while?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank You for so often coming alongside me and lifting me up with Your word. Cleanse my lips, so that my words are no longer only about expressing myself but about building up others. Give me the wisdom to discern who needs a reminder, who needs encouragement, and who needs me to reach out a hand to help. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, think of a brother or sister who is discouraged and send them a message to “run alongside” them: tell them you remember what they are going through and that you are praying for them, and include a verse you would like to give them right now.
lessons.quick: One sentence can tear down a wall or build a house; I choose to build.
text: Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do.
But we beg you, brothers, to know those who labor among you, and are over you in the Lord and admonish you,
and to respect and honor them in love for their work’s sake. Be at peace among yourselves.
We exhort you, brothers: Admonish the disorderly; encourage the faint-hearted; support the weak; be patient toward all.
See that no one returns evil for evil to anyone, but always follow after that which is good for one another and for all.

lessons.title: While It Is Still Called Today
lessons.hear:
There was a brother in a small group who began missing meetings after he changed jobs. At first everyone thought, “He must be busy; let’s not put pressure on him.” One month passed, then two, and no one asked. Six months later the group leader finally invited him for coffee. He said flatly, “Honestly, I stopped praying a long time ago. Believing or not believing doesn’t seem to make much difference. Anyway, it didn’t seem like anyone cared whether I came.”

We often hold two old mindsets. One says, “Faith is a private matter; don’t interfere in other people’s lives.” The other says, “Encouraging people is the pastor’s and the small group leader’s job; I’m not spiritual enough.” So everyone stays very polite and very quiet, and watches a fellow member slowly drift away.

The writer of Hebrews takes this very seriously: “exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called ‘today’, lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13). Notice three words. “Day by day”—encouragement is not one big talk a year but small everyday reminders. “One another”—not only leaders speaking to the congregation, but every member to every member. “Hardened”—a heart doesn’t harden overnight; it sets slowly, like concrete. While it is still soft, a single sentence can change its direction.

God’s perspective is that silence isn’t always respect; sometimes it is indifference. Real love is willing to risk a little rejection to ask, “How have you been lately? I’ve missed you.” The same writer says, “Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works” (Hebrews 10:24).

That brother later said that what brought him back wasn’t a sermon but the first question his leader asked when they sat down that day. The sentence you speak today could be the one that reaches someone before their heart sets.
lessons.light: Self-centered people fear the hassle, fear rejection, and fear being called nosy, so they choose silence. Selfless people shift their focus from their own face to the other person’s soul. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than saving face. Change your perspective: from “That’s none of my business” to “He is part of my body.”
think: Why does Hebrews 3:12-14 stress “day by day” and “so long as it is called ‘today’”?
Do I use “respect” or “not being spiritual enough” as an excuse for staying silent?
Which brother or sister who has been gradually fading away should I reach out to today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often call it respect when really I am afraid of the hassle or of being rejected, and I watch brothers and sisters drift away without saying a word. Give me courage and gentleness to care for them while it is still called today. May my words reach them while their hearts are still soft and bring them back to You. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, identify a brother or sister who has been coming less often or has gone quiet in the group chat. Call or message them personally: “How are you doing? I was thinking of you, and I prayed for you.” Don’t press for reasons; simply express that you care.
lessons.quick: Silence isn’t always respect; while it is still today, speak a word of care.
text: Beware, brothers, lest perhaps there might be in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, in falling away from the living God;
but exhort one another day by day, so long as it is called “today”, lest any one of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
For we have become partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence firm to the end,

lessons.title: Words That Fit the Need
lessons.hear:
Paul’s guidelines for how the church speaks point in two directions. On one hand: “putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbor. For we are members of one another” (Ephesians 4:25). On the other: “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29). True words and good words—we need both. True words without good words become a knife; good words without true words become sugarcoating.

The phrase “as the need may be” is worth reading slowly. It means according to what the moment calls for. The same sentence lands completely differently with someone who just lost a job and someone who just got promoted. Proverbs says, “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver” (Proverbs 25:11). Good words aren’t fancy words; they are fitting words—what this person needs to hear, at the right time.

Today, practice speaking one sentence that builds someone up. You can prepare in three steps:
First, see specifically: instead of just saying, “You’re great,” say, “I’ve noticed you always come early to help set up the chairs.” When you are specific, the other person knows you have really seen them.
Second, connect it to God: name the grace of God you see in it—for example, “I see the Lord’s faithfulness in you.” This affirms not a person’s performance but God’s work.
Third, send a blessing: a short prayer or a verse, so your words don’t stop with you but point to the Lord.

You can write it on a card, send a message, or say it face to face. Don’t underestimate a single sentence. Many people have made it through a discouraging night because of a little card someone wrote them.
lessons.light: Keep the focus on Jesus, not on yourself and not on others. Words that build people up aren’t flattery, and they aren’t a showcase for your eloquence; they turn people’s eyes toward Christ. Speak from the heart, and you will speak truth and grace blended by the Holy Spirit; speak only from the head, and often all that’s left is criticism and empty politeness.
think: How do Ephesians 4:25 and 4:29 each tell us to speak, and how do the two balance each other?
Do I more easily speak only truth until it becomes a knife, or only pleasant words until they become sugarcoating?
To whom will I speak today using “see specifically, connect it to God, send a blessing”?
lessons.speak: Lord, govern my tongue. I have often spoken true words that wound and polite words that are empty. Today teach me to speak what is good for building others up as the need may be, to see specifically the grace in my brothers and sisters, and to give the glory to You. May my words be apples of gold that give grace to those who hear. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, use the three steps—see specifically, connect it to God, send a blessing—to write a card or message to a ministry team member who serves quietly, and send it before tonight.
lessons.quick: Speak the truth and speak what is good, with fitting words at the right time.
text: Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbor, for we are members of one another.
“Be angry, and don’t sin.” Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath,
and don’t give place to the devil.
Let him who stole steal no more; but rather let him labor, producing with his hands something that is good, that he may have something to give to him who has need.
Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.

lessons.title: Job’s Friends
lessons.hear:
Job’s three friends started out remarkably well. When they heard about Job’s disaster, they came from far away, and “they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great” (Job 2:13). Those seven days of silence were the most beautiful comfort they offered in the whole book of Job.

The trouble began when they opened their mouths. They had plenty of correct theological vocabulary, but they rushed to explain why Job was suffering, hinting round after round that he must have offended God somewhere. In his pain Job said, “You are all miserable comforters!” (Job 16:2). In the end God Himself spoke, telling them, “You have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has” (Job 42:8).

This is a mirror. The church often has this kind of “encouragement” too. A sister has a miscarriage, and someone asks whether her faith wasn’t strong enough. A brother loses his job, and someone hurries to hand him a set of spiritual principles. A newcomer is weeping in grief, and we are busy correcting their theology. We think we are building people up, but we are actually adding to their load. Proverbs puts it well: “There is one who speaks rashly like the piercing of a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals” (Proverbs 12:18).

Review yourself: Am I quick to give answers instead of first being present? Is my encouragement meant to help the other person, or to prove that I’m right? Do I only offer opinions, while rarely praying for them?

The story ends full of grace. The friends offered sacrifices and admitted their wrong as God commanded, and Job “prayed for his friends” (Job 42:10). Those who spoke wrongly can be restored, and the one who was hurt can intercede for those who hurt him. The first step of adjustment is often to say a little less, stay a little longer, and pray a little more.
lessons.light: Pride often hides inside “I need to give you the answer,” as if I stood in God’s place and could explain everything. Humility returns to our proper place, admitting there are things I don’t understand and that I can only go with you before God. Life first, then relationships: first a life of presence, and then our words will have power to build.
think: In what way did Job’s friends do well, and where did they fail?
Have I ever wounded someone who was suffering with “correct doctrine”?
The next time I face a suffering brother or sister, what will I do first, and what will I say less of?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I am often quick to give answers and quick to correct, and I forget to simply be present first. Forgive me for the times I have wounded others with words that were correct but rash. Give me the tongue of the wise that brings healing; help me say a little less, stay a little longer, and pray for others a little more. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a brother or sister you have hurt with your words, and apologize to them privately today without defending yourself. If no one comes to mind, then the next time someone pours out their heart to you, listen all the way through and pray for them first, without rushing to give advice.
lessons.quick: Be present first, then speak; fewer answers, more prayer.
text: It was so, that after the LORD had spoken these words to Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My wrath is kindled against you, and against your two friends; for you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.

Now therefore, take to yourselves seven bulls and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and offer up for yourselves a burnt offering; and my servant Job shall pray for you, for I will accept him, that I not deal with you according to your folly. For you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.”
So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went and did what the LORD commanded them, and the LORD accepted Job.
The LORD restored Job’s prosperity when he prayed for his friends. The LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before.

lessons.title: Becoming Someone’s Barnabas
lessons.hear:
In the early church there was a brother whose given name was Joseph, but the apostles gave him a nickname: “Barnabas (which is, being interpreted, Son of Encouragement)” (Acts 4:36). What people remembered him for wasn’t a title but the fact that he was always lifting others up.

When Saul first came to faith, the disciples were afraid of him and didn’t believe he was a disciple, “but Barnabas took him, and brought him to the apostles” (Acts 9:27). Later, when a group of new believers appeared in Antioch, the church in Jerusalem sent Barnabas. When he arrived “and had seen the grace of God, was glad. He exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord.” (Acts 11:23). Notice the order: first he saw grace, then he rejoiced, then he encouraged. Next he did something remarkably far-sighted: “Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul” (Acts 11:25), bringing into ministry a brother whom few people valued at the time. That Saul, of course, became Paul.

This week we have learned that encouragement means coming alongside someone and running with them; that we should exhort one another day by day, while it is still called today; that we speak both truth and good words; and that we are present first, then speak. Barnabas lived all of this out—and his encouragement multiplied. The man he lifted up went on to lift up churches across the whole Gentile world.

Multiplying encouragement means going to “look for Saul.” In your church there may be someone who is easily overlooked, who once fell, or who is new in the faith—someone people still hesitate to get close to. Will you be their Barnabas? Welcome them, speak up for them, bring them along to serve. You don’t have to become Paul, but you can be the one who found Paul.
lessons.light: The “3” of 235 is about building relationships of spiritual parents and children; Barnabas was Paul’s spiritual sponsor and supporter. The final step in the eight steps of changing a mindset is multiplication: truth doesn’t stop with me but passes on to the next person through a word I speak or a welcome I extend.
think: What did Barnabas see first in Antioch, and what did he do next?
Is there someone near me who, like Saul, no one yet dares to get close to?
How will I become someone’s Barnabas this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank You for lifting me up through the words of certain people. Make me a Barnabas to others: glad when I see Your grace in people, willing to welcome those who have not yet been valued, and bringing them along to serve. May my encouragement keep multiplying so that Your church is built up. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite someone who is new in the faith, has fallen, or is often overlooked to have tea with you. Listen to their story, share one verse from this week, and invite them to join you next time in an area of service.
lessons.quick: You don’t have to be Paul, but you can be the Barnabas who found him.
text: The report concerning them came to the ears of the assembly which was in Jerusalem. They sent out Barnabas to go as far as Antioch,
who, when he had come, and had seen the grace of God, was glad. He exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they should remain near to the Lord.
For he was a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith, and many people were added to the Lord.
Barnabas went out to Tarsus to look for Saul.
When he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they were gathered together with the assembly, and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.

weeks.title: Where Conflict Comes From
weeks.keyText: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
weeks.theme: Quarrels on the outside often begin with desires on the inside; the first step toward reconciliation is to look at myself.
group: Read James 4:1-6. Where does James say wars and fightings come from? How does this differ from the way we usually think?
Think back to a dispute in your church or small group. Beneath all the “reasons,” what did you really want in your heart?
This week, each person chooses one ongoing source of friction and first examines themselves before God; at the next small group meeting, pray for one another.
weeks.sunday: Before you walk into the sanctuary this Lord’s Day, ask yourself, “Who have I had friction with lately, and what is it that I want?” During worship, hand this matter over to the Lord to reign over. If you see that brother or sister during the service, don’t rush to negotiate; simply ask the Lord to soften your heart. Afterward, pray a sentence of blessing for them.

lessons.title: The Battlefield Is Within
lessons.hear:
Starting this week, we turn to a very real subject: conflict and reconciliation. Whenever a group of people come together, there will be conflict—the ministry team argues over the budget, the choir is unhappy about song choices, one comment in the group chat sets off a chain of replies. James opens with a direct question: “Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?” (James 4:1).

James pulls our gaze from the outside to the inside. We assume conflict comes from the other person: he’s too domineering, she’s too sensitive, that decision was too hasty. But James says that before the war breaks out on the outside, a war is already raging within: “You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war.” (James 4:2). I want to be respected, I want things done my way, I want my ministry to be valued—and when I can’t get what I want, it turns into envy, and then erupts through my mouth and my hands. Proverbs names the root in one line: “Pride only breeds quarrels” (Proverbs 13:10).

This doesn’t mean every disagreement is sin. It’s normal for people to see things differently and to have different gifts; that is even part of the richness of the body. But when a disagreement turns into “I have to win,” when we start keeping score, forming alliances, and giving each other the cold shoulder, we need to ask: who is reigning inside me—Jesus, or my own desires?

The good news is in verse 6: “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (James 4:6). God doesn’t merely diagnose the disease; He also provides the cure. However great the conflict, grace is greater. For today, you don’t need to deal with the other person. Just ask the Holy Spirit to shine His light on the battlefield inside you.
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our proper place and grasping power; many church conflicts, at bottom, are fights over “who gets the final say.” Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Change begins with me: first look at the desires inside me, not at the faults outside in others.
think: In James 4:1-6, how does conflict develop, layer by layer?
In the last conflict that made me angry, what was it that I couldn’t get?
How will I hand that “want” over to the Lord today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I often assume conflicts are caused by others. Today, shine Your light on the battlefield within me. I confess that I too want to be respected, want things my way, and want to win. Give me more grace and humble me, so that You reign in my heart and my desires do not. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the most recent conflict that left you uncomfortable. Beside it, honestly add the sentence, “In this situation, what I really wanted was…,” and then bring that sheet of paper to the Lord in prayer.
lessons.quick: The war outside often starts with the desires inside.
text: Where do wars and fightings among you come from? Don’t they come from your pleasures that war in your members?
You lust, and don’t have. You murder and covet, and can’t obtain. You fight and make war. You don’t have, because you don’t ask.
You ask, and don’t receive, because you ask with wrong motives, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.
You adulterers and adulteresses, don’t you know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Whoever therefore wants to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
Or do you think that the Scripture says in vain, “The Spirit who lives in us yearns jealously”?
But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

lessons.title: “I Follow Paul”
lessons.hear:
A church welcomed a new pastor. He brought a new style of worship and a new small group structure, and some longtime older members found it hard to adjust. They often said, “The old pastor didn’t do it this way.” The younger people felt the older members were stuck in the past and out of touch. After a year, the Sunday congregation had split into two circles—courteous to each other, but no longer sharing meals. Both sides believed they were acting for the good of the church.

Our old mindset says: conflict happens because of different philosophies; I’m fighting for truth, for direction, for the good of the church. But Paul told the church in Corinth, “You are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?” (1 Corinthians 3:3). The Corinthians had split into “I follow Paul” and “I follow Apollos.” On the surface they were debating which preacher was better, but Paul went straight to the heart of it: this is fleshly, the behavior of babies.

God’s perspective is convicting: many disputes wear spiritual clothing, but underneath are human preferences, human loyalties, and human pride. We rarely argue about the doctrine of the Trinity, yet we often damage our unity over the style of worship music, the seating arrangement, or who got told first.

Of course, some matters really do involve truth and justice. Paul himself “resisted [Peter] to his face” for the sake of the truth of the gospel (Galatians 2:11), and when facing abuse of power or injustice, we should not stay silent in the name of peace. But even when we speak up for truth, we must first examine ourselves: is my motive to let Christ reign, or to let me win? The turning point for that church came when an older member said at a prayer meeting, “Lord, I’ve realized it isn’t the old pastor I can’t let go of—it’s the comfortable place I was used to.”
lessons.light: Fleshly people are centered on people, forming factions and attaching themselves to a person; spiritual people are centered on Christ, with their focus on Jesus rather than on any person. Shift from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one: Paul and Apollos are only servants, and it is God who gives the growth. When Jesus reigns, there is no “our side.”
think: In 1 Corinthians 3:1-4, on what basis does Paul say the Corinthians are fleshly?
Do I belong to some kind of “I follow so-and-so” camp or circle at church?
Beneath a position I insist on, are my preferences or my pride hiding?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often call my preferences truth and treat my own circle as if it were the church. Shine Your light on my motives in disputes, and help me discern what is truth and what is merely habit. Remove the fleshly jealousy and strife in me, and let Christ reign among us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, identify one thing you insist on at church and write two columns: “This is a biblical principle” and “This is my preference or habit.” Sort it honestly, then hand it over to the Lord.
lessons.quick: Many disputes wear spiritual clothing, but underneath are my preferences and my pride.
text: Brothers, I couldn’t speak to you as to spiritual, but as to fleshly, as to babies in Christ.
I fed you with milk, not with solid food, for you weren’t yet ready. Indeed, you aren’t ready even now,
for you are still fleshly. For insofar as there is jealousy, strife, and factions among you, aren’t you fleshly, and don’t you walk in the ways of men?
For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” aren’t you fleshly?

lessons.title: Before You Speak, Go to God
lessons.hear:
When conflict arises, our most natural reaction is to respond immediately: type a long paragraph in the group chat, find someone to vent to, or simply go silent. James gives a completely different order: go to God first, then to people. He says, “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (James 4:8), and “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10).

Today, take one ongoing source of friction, and before you say anything, do four things based on this passage:
First, submit to God: tell the Lord, “In this matter, You reign, not me.” This hands over control of how the conflict is handled.
Second, resist the devil: the devil loves to fan the flames in conflict. Don’t pass things along, don’t pull people onto your side, and don’t vent in the group chat. Proverbs says, “Without gossip, a quarrel dies down” (Proverbs 26:20).
Third, draw near to God and purify your heart: ask yourself before the Lord, What is it that I want? Where did I speak harshly or exaggerate the other person’s fault?
Fourth, humble yourself before the Lord: admit your own part, and ask the Lord to change you, rather than first asking Him to change them.

After these four steps, decide whether to speak and how. You will usually find you have less to say, and your tone has softened. Earlier, James also urged us: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19).

One caution: “looking at myself first” doesn’t mean taking all the blame, nor does it mean the person who was hurt should suffer in silence. If the conflict involves oppression, abuse of power, or any form of violence, please seek help from trustworthy elders and deacons, a supervising church body, or professionals. We go to God first so that we can take the next step with a clean heart and a clear head.
lessons.light: Use your heart and rely on the Holy Spirit, not your head and yourself. Handling conflict with your head means replaying the other person’s faults over and over and rehearsing your comeback, growing more upset the more you think. Relying on the Holy Spirit with your heart means first handing control to Jesus; then your heart grows quiet and your words are seasoned. Humility isn’t losing; it is returning to our proper place and letting God be God.
think: In James 4:7-10, which actions are directed toward God, and which toward ourselves?
When I face conflict, what is my most common first reaction?
Which source of friction will I bring before God today using these four steps?
lessons.speak: Lord, I bring this friction before You. In this matter You reign, not me. Guard my mouth so that I don’t pass things along or pull people onto my side. Purify my heart and show me my own part, and change me first. Give me the wisdom to be swift to hear and slow to speak. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, as you face an ongoing source of friction, before replying to any message or saying anything, spend ten minutes praying through the four steps—submit, resist, draw near, humble yourself—and then decide what to say.
lessons.quick: Before you speak, go to God; ask the Lord to change me first.
text: Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners. Purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Lament, mourn, and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.

lessons.title: Even Co-Workers Part Ways
lessons.hear:
If you think only unspiritual people have conflicts, look at Paul and Barnabas. They were sent out together by the Holy Spirit, endured persecution together, and together testified at the Jerusalem Council for the freedom of the Gentiles. Yet just before their second journey, over whether to take Mark along, “the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other” (Acts 15:39).

Scripture doesn’t cover for them, and it doesn’t say outright who was right. Paul’s priority was the mission: Mark had deserted them partway through and couldn’t be relied on. Barnabas’s priority was the person: this young man needed a second chance. Both had a point, but the word “contention” in the original carries a sense of something fierce and sharp. Two good men, each holding a piece of the truth, argued until they went their separate ways.

This mirror is well suited for today’s review. In my conflict, has some part of “I have a point” gradually turned into “I have to win”? Do I see only the values I care about, while failing to see the values the other person cares about? Have I turned one disagreement into a final verdict on a person?

What followed brings hope. Years later, Paul still mentions Barnabas in his letters as a co-worker who labored just as he did (see 1 Corinthians 9:6). And Mark, the one Paul had once refused, was singled out by Paul near the end of his life: “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). People grow, views get corrected, and over time the Lord can heal relationships.

The direction for adjustment is this: admit that I may be seeing only half the picture; put into words the value the other person cares about, and respect it; and don’t treat today’s disagreement as a permanent verdict on that person.
lessons.light: Pride lets me see only my half of the truth and demand that others accept it completely; humility admits, “What I see is limited, and what you see has value too.” People matter more than tasks—even when we disagree about a task, we must not hurt or dismiss a person over it.
think: What did Paul and Barnabas each care about most, and what hope do later passages reveal?
In my most recent dispute, did “I have a point” turn into “I have to win”?
How can I put into words, and respect, the value the other person cares about?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, You know that in disputes I often see only my half and then demand that others accept all of it. Forgive me for turning disagreements into verdicts on people. Give me a humble heart to see the value the other person holds, and in time, heal my relationship with that brother or sister. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a brother or sister you have clashed with, and write one sentence: “In that matter, what they cared about was…, and that has real value too.” If appropriate, find a chance this week to tell them this word of affirmation.
lessons.quick: I see only half; what you care about has value too.
text: After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.”
Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.
He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.

lessons.title: Let There Be No Strife Between Us
lessons.hear:
Abram and his nephew Lot left their homeland together and shared both the good times and the hard times. Later, as both households’ flocks and herds multiplied, “the land was not able to bear them,” and the herdsmen on both sides began to quarrel (Genesis 13:6-7). The cause of the conflict was ordinary: limited resources, and everyone wanted the best pasture. It is really no different from churches arguing over rooms, budgets, and meeting times.

As the elder, and as the one who had received God’s promise, Abram could easily have chosen first. Instead he said, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives.” (Genesis 13:8). Then he handed the choice to Lot: “If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left” (Genesis 13:9). Abram was willing to take the short end of the deal, because he valued the relationship and his security was in God’s hands. Lot chose by sight, picking the well-watered plain, and step by step moved his tent toward Sodom. Abram stayed where he was, yet God told him that all the land he could see would be given to him (see Genesis 13:14-15). The one who gave way lost nothing, because God was his inheritance.

This week we have seen that conflict often begins with desires inside us; that many disputes wear spiritual clothing while underneath are preferences and pride; that we should go to God before we speak; and that even good co-workers can part ways, yet God can heal over time. Abram shows us a simple yet powerful response: we are family, so we will not fight.

Multiplication means passing on this culture of looking at ourselves first and being willing to give way. Your children watch how you handle arguments at home; your small group members watch how you respond to differing views in ministry meetings. When they see you examine yourself first, refuse to pull people onto your side, and give way for the sake of the relationship, they learn the most fundamental lesson of reconciliation. Next, we will learn to take the initiative to go to a brother or sister and be reconciled.
lessons.light: Humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Abram laid down his right to choose and returned to his proper place of trusting God, and as a result God Himself became his inheritance. Selflessness isn’t loss; it is entering into the limitless: I give up one pasture, and God gives me the whole Promised Land.
think: On what basis did Abram urge Lot not to quarrel, and how did he handle the right to choose?
In what areas do I find it hard to give way first, as Abram did?
With whom will I share what I’ve learned this week about looking at myself first?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank You for shining Your light on the battlefield inside me this week. I want to learn from Abram: to value relationships above pastures and to place my security in Your hands. Make me, at home and at church, someone who examines myself first and is willing to give way, and help me pass this heart of reconciliation on to the next generation. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This weekend, sit down with a family member, a spiritual companion, or a small group member and share the line, “Quarrels on the outside often begin with desires on the inside.” Each of you name one thing you are willing to give way on first, and pray for each other.
lessons.quick: We are family, so we don’t fight; for the one who gives way, God is the inheritance.
text: Lot also, who went with Abram, had flocks, herds, and tents.
The land was not able to bear them, that they might live together; for their possessions were so great that they couldn’t live together.
There was strife between the herdsmen of Abram’s livestock and the herdsmen of Lot’s livestock. The Canaanites and the Perizzites lived in the land at that time.
Abram said to Lot, “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives.
Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left.”

Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere, before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, as you go to Zoar.
So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one another.
Abram lived in the land of Canaan, and Lot lived in the cities of the plain, and moved his tent as far as Sodom.

weeks.title: First Be Reconciled to Your Brother
weeks.keyText: leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
weeks.theme: God cares more about my relationship with my brother than about the gift I lay on the altar; whoever is reminded gets up first.
group: Read Matthew 5:23-24. Why does Jesus tell people to leave their gift at the altar, and how does that strike you?
What usually keeps you from going first to make peace—pride, fear of awkwardness, or the feeling that it isn’t your fault?
Toward whom are you willing to take a first step of reconciliation this week, and how can the small group pray for you and walk with you?
weeks.sunday: Before you walk into church this Sunday, pause as Jesus said: Is there a brother or sister who has something against me? If someone comes to mind, settle it in your heart to go and make peace this week. During the offering or Communion, place that relationship in the Lord’s hands; and if that person is there after the service, go and greet them first, even with just a nod and a hello.

lessons.title: Leave Your Gift at the Altar
lessons.hear:
Picture the scene. A Jewish man has walked for days from Galilee, leading a lamb to Jerusalem. He has waited in line a long time, and at last he stands before the altar. Just as he is about to offer his sacrifice, he suddenly remembers: back home there is a brother who holds a grudge against him. Jesus says the right thing to do now is not to hurry up, finish the offering, and deal with it later. Instead: “leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24).

That is a startling statement. In the minds of Jesus’ listeners, offering sacrifice was the holiest thing a person could do. Yet Jesus says one thing comes even before it—being reconciled to your brother. Notice that the text does not say “if you have something against your brother,” but “there remember that your brother has anything against you” (Matthew 5:23). Even if you feel the fault is not entirely yours, the Lord still wants you to get up first. The initiative in reconciliation does not belong to the one who was wronged, nor to the one who did wrong, but to the one whom the Holy Spirit reminds first.

Jesus places these words inside his teaching on “You shall not murder.” Murder, he says, is rooted in the heart: in anger, in calling a brother “Raca”—a worthless good-for-nothing—or calling him “You fool!” Few of us ever pick up a knife. But we often “dispose of” a brother in our hearts—with coldness, with a remark behind his back, with years of silence. God looks at the heart.

So worship and relationships cannot be separated. You can raise your hands and sing on Sunday while not having said hello for three years to the ministry co-worker sitting three rows behind you. In God’s eyes, there is a part of that song you haven’t finished singing. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you: Is there a gift I need to leave at the altar first?
lessons.light: The order of relationships is God first, then people. But if my relationship with God is real, it will surely flow into my relationships with people. The self-centered person says, “I’ll wait for him to apologize first.” The selfless person hears the Lord say “go first” and gets up. To let Jesus reign is to let him decide who takes the first step—and he often points at me.
think: In Matthew 5:21-26, which commandment does Jesus connect with anger?
Is there a member of the body whom I have “disposed of” in my heart and haven’t spoken with for years?
If the Holy Spirit brings a name to mind today, how am I willing to “go first”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you care more about my relationship with my brother than about the gift I bring to the altar. I confess that I often try to cover unresolved resentment with more service and more giving. Holy Spirit, shine your light on me; bring to mind the people I need to be reconciled with, and give me the courage to get up first. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Take five quiet minutes today and ask the Holy Spirit to bring to mind a brother or sister with whom you have unresolved tension. Write down the name, and beside it write: “Lord, I am willing to go first.” Choose a time this week to reach out to them.
lessons.quick: The gift can wait; reconciliation can’t—whoever is reminded gets up first.
text: “You have heard that it was said to the ancient ones, ‘You shall not murder;’ and ‘Whoever murders will be in danger of the judgment.’

But I tell you that everyone who is angry with his brother without a cause will be in danger of the judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca!’ will be in danger of the council. Whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be in danger of the fire of Gehenna.
“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you,
leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
Agree with your adversary quickly while you are with him on the way; lest perhaps the prosecutor deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison.
Most certainly I tell you, you shall by no means get out of there until you have paid the last penny.

lessons.title: First Remove Your Own Beam
lessons.hear:
A brother in a small group had reached a stalemate with the co-worker who led worship. He told his small group leader all about it: how that co-worker didn’t respect people, changed songs at the last minute, and made barbed comments in the group chat. The leader listened and asked just one question: “In all this, what part do you think you need to confess to the Lord?” He was speechless for a long time. Only that night, back at home, did he remember that he too had posted a hurtful reply in the group chat—and had privately complained about that co-worker to three different people.

Our old mindset says, “Of course reconciliation is good, but first the other person has to admit he was wrong.” We keep a ledger in our hearts that records, in sharp detail, what others owe us, while what we owe others stays blurry. Jesus punctures this blind spot with an almost comical picture: “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3). A man with a wooden beam sticking out of his eye is holding a pair of tweezers, trying to pick a speck out of someone else’s.

God’s perspective is this: “First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Matthew 7:5). Notice that Jesus does not say the brother’s speck doesn’t exist, nor that we may never help remove it. What he speaks of is order—deal with yourself first. When I first admit my own part, my eyes see clearly, my heart grows soft, and the words I speak can help rather than wound.

In a conflict, each side often has both a beam and a speck. If both people wait for the other to pull theirs out first, the church will be left with two wooden beams standing forever. But if one person bows first and says, “I was wrong in this too—I’m sorry,” it often opens the floodgates, and the other person’s heart softens as well. Change begins with me.
lessons.light: Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Fixing my eyes on someone else’s speck is taking a seat on the judge’s bench; seeing my own beam is returning to my proper place as a sinner who has received grace. The focus is on Jesus, not on others: when I see myself in the Lord’s light, I am no longer in a hurry to judge my brother.
think: In Matthew 7:1-5, what picture does Jesus use to describe those who judge others?
In a tense relationship right now, what might my own “beam” be?
How can I acknowledge my own part first, in a single sentence?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I am very good at seeing other people’s specks but blind to my own beam. Holy Spirit, shine your light on the words I have spoken and the attitudes I have held in this conflict, and let me confess my sin to you first. Give me a humble heart, so that I can bow first and help my brother with gentleness. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Take a sheet of paper and divide one tense relationship into two columns: “His speck” and “My beam.” Today fill in only the right-hand column—write down at least two things—and then confess each one to the Lord.
lessons.quick: Remove your own beam first; then your eyes see clearly and your heart grows soft.
text: “Don’t judge, so that you won’t be judged.
For with whatever judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with whatever measure you measure, it will be measured to you.
Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?
Or how will you tell your brother, ‘Let me remove the speck from your eye,’ and behold, the beam is in your own eye?
You hypocrite! First remove the beam out of your own eye, and then you can see clearly to remove the speck out of your brother’s eye.

lessons.title: At Peace with All People
lessons.hear:
Paul is very practical: “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18). This sentence has two emphases. “If it is possible” admits that reconciliation can’t be accomplished by one side’s wishes alone—the other person may refuse or may not be ready yet, and sometimes safety is involved and distance is needed. But “as much as it is up to you” means that within what I can do, I am to give it my very best effort.

So what can I do today? Here are three simple steps.
1. Pray before you speak. Ask the Lord to prepare the other person’s heart and to prepare your own mouth, so that you don’t go in looking to settle the score.
2. Apologize for your part, with no “but.” “At the last meeting my tone was harsh and I embarrassed you. I’m sorry.” One apology without a “but” carries more power than ten explanations.
3. Say that you value the relationship. “You’re my brother, and I don’t want this to keep standing between us.”

If the other person isn’t ready to respond, don’t force it. Paul says, “Repay no one evil for evil” (Romans 12:17), and again, “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21). You can keep praying for him, greet him kindly at church, and leave the outcome with God. Vengeance belongs to the Lord; you don’t need to win.

The wise men of the Old Testament said long ago, “A brother offended is more difficult than a fortified city” (Proverbs 18:19). Precisely because it is so hard, we need to knock on that door earlier, more lightly, and more gently. Go and knock today.
lessons.light: The “2” in 920 includes the person I find hardest to get along with. Self-centered peace says, “You step back first, then I will.” Selfless peace says, “I’ll do all I can and leave the rest to the Lord.” Overcoming evil with good is not weakness; it is letting Jesus reign in this relationship instead of letting evil take charge.
think: In Romans 12:17-21, what “don’ts” and “dos” does Paul give?
When it comes to reconciliation, what “buts” do I tend to add after an apology?
What apology without a “but” will I start with today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you accomplished reconciliation for us, and I want to be a peacemaker too. Today give me courage to contact that brother or sister. Rule over my tongue so that I speak only words that build up. If he isn’t ready yet, keep me from being overcome by evil, and help me keep treating him with good. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Before nine o’clock tonight, send a message to or call the person whose name you wrote down. Apologize for your part in one sentence with no “but,” and set a time to meet for coffee.
lessons.quick: Do all I can, offer an apology with no “but,” and leave the rest to the Lord.
text: Repay no one evil for evil. Respect what is honorable in the sight of all men.
If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.
Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, “Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.”
Therefore “If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him a drink; for in doing so, you will heap coals of fire on his head.”
Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

lessons.title: Jacob Returns to Esau
lessons.hear:
Jacob and Esau were brothers estranged for twenty years. Jacob had cheated Esau out of his birthright and his blessing; Esau vowed to kill him, and Jacob had to flee to a distant land. Twenty years later, God told him to go home—and the road home led straight toward the brother he had wronged.

Jacob’s preparations are worth reviewing. On the one hand, he really was moving toward reconciliation: he prepared a generous gift, called his brother “my lord,” and “bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother” (Genesis 33:3). On the other hand, his heart was still full of calculation. He arranged his family in ranks, putting his beloved Rachel and Joseph at the very back so they could escape if things went wrong. That looks a lot like us: willing to reconcile, yet keeping an escape route; saying sorry, yet still privately calculating our losses and our face.

The turning point came the night before. At the ford of the Jabbok, Jacob wrestled with God; his hip was touched, and from then on he limped (see Genesis 32:24-31). The man who walked toward Esau the next day was no longer the Jacob who won by cleverness, but a man God had touched, limping along. The power to reconcile often doesn’t come from how thoroughly we have prepared, but from being broken before God first.

The outcome was beyond anything he expected: “Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept” (Genesis 33:4). And Jacob said something beautiful: “I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God” (Genesis 33:10).

Today, review your own heart: In the relationship I want to mend, what am I still calculating? Am I bringing a gift to “smooth things over,” or bringing a heart broken by the Lord to “come back”? If an earlier attempt failed, don’t lose heart. The way to adjust is to go back to God and wrestle with him first—then get up and go.
lessons.light: The self-centered Jacob lived by calculation; Israel, with his new name, lived by God. Dealing with God before reconciling with people—this is the order of relationships: God first, then people. The limp from God’s touch is not a mark of failure but a mark of victory: I no longer rely on myself, but walk toward my brother leaning on the Lord.
think: In Genesis 33:1-11, what did Jacob and Esau each do, and which action moves you most?
In seeking reconciliation, what “escape routes” and calculations am I still holding on to?
Before I walk toward my brother again, what do I need to settle with the Lord first?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, like Jacob I often try to fix my relationships with my own cleverness. Touch the place in my heart that refuses to let go; break me, so that I can walk toward my brother with a soft heart. If my efforts have failed before, heal my discouragement and give me the courage to come back again. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Look back on the steps toward reconciliation you have taken these past few days, and write down which words came from the Lord and which came from calculation. Tonight, spend ten minutes bringing these to the Lord and ask him to adjust your next step.
lessons.quick: Be broken by God first, then walk toward your brother—only a limping Jacob can embrace Esau.
text: Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, Esau was coming, and with him four hundred men. He divided the children between Leah, Rachel, and the two servants.
He put the servants and their children in front, Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear.
He himself passed over in front of them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
He lifted up his eyes, and saw the women and the children; and said, “Who are these with you?” He said, “The children whom God has graciously given your servant.”
