Then the servants came near with their children, and they bowed themselves.
Leah also and her children came near, and bowed themselves. After them, Joseph came near with Rachel, and they bowed themselves.
Esau said, “What do you mean by all this company which I met?” Jacob said, “To find favor in the sight of my lord.”
Esau said, “I have enough, my brother; let that which you have be yours.”
Jacob said, “Please, no, if I have now found favor in your sight, then receive my present at my hand, because I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me.
Please take the gift that I brought to you, because God has dealt graciously with me, and because I have enough.” He urged him, and he took it.

lessons.title: Ambassadors of Reconciliation
lessons.hear:
This week we have been learning about reconciliation, and its deepest root is not people skills but the gospel itself. Paul says, “But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18).

First, see the grace. While we were still God’s enemies, it was God who first “left the altar” and came to us himself. He did not wait for us to apologize first; he sent his Son, who tore down the dividing wall on the cross. I can take the initiative toward my brother because God first took the initiative toward me. Those who go to make peace are those who have first been reconciled.

Then, see the commission. God has “committed to us the word of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:19). The church is not only a group of people who have been reconciled to God; it is also a group of people entrusted with bringing about reconciliation. One small group leader shared how two sisters in her group had fallen out over the division of a ministry task. She didn’t carry messages back and forth between them. Instead she prayed with each of them separately, and finally invited the two of them to a meal, sitting between them and doing nothing but pouring tea and praying. By the end of that meal, both of them were in tears.

Multiplication means letting reconciliation flow out through you. Perhaps this week you have already taken a step toward a brother or sister. Tell your story—including the fear, the struggle, and the Lord’s help—to someone else who is stuck in a relationship. You don’t need to give him answers; just tell him, “I was stuck too, but the Lord helped me go first.” Your testimony may be the very word that gets him up on his feet.
lessons.light: Change begins with me, but it doesn’t stop with me. When our mindset changes, our life and living change, and finally our relationships are renewed. Every relationship that is restored is one more brick laid in God’s system on earth. Being Christ’s ambassadors means letting people see, in our reconciliation, the Lord who reconciles people to God.
think: How many times does “reconcile” or “reconciliation” appear in 2 Corinthians 5:17-20, and who takes the initiative?
What did I experience this week in the area of reconciliation, and what am I most thankful to the Lord for?
With whom can I share this experience, to encourage him to get up and go?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you that while I was still your enemy, you first reconciled me to yourself through Christ. Let this grace be my strength. Make me someone who brings about reconciliation in the church—not carrying gossip, not stirring up trouble, but passing on your peace. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Sometime this week, meet with your spiritual companion and spend ten minutes sharing your journey toward reconciliation (whether it succeeded or is still in progress). Then pray together for a relationship that still needs to be restored.
lessons.quick: Those who have been reconciled are entrusted with bringing reconciliation.
text: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.
But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation;
namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses, and having committed to us the word of reconciliation.
We are therefore ambassadors on behalf of Christ, as though God were entreating by us: we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.

weeks.title: The Matthew 18 Path to Reconciliation
weeks.keyText: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.
weeks.theme: When we go to a brother who has done wrong, the goal is to gain him back, not to win an argument.
group: Read Matthew 18:15-17. What is the shared goal of all three steps, and which sentence stands out to you most?
When you’ve been wronged in the past, did you usually go to the person first or tell someone else first—and why?
Is there a small matter this week that you are willing to raise privately and gently, the Lord’s way, and how can the small group pray for you?
weeks.sunday: Before the service this Sunday, ask the Lord to search you: Have I recently been talking about a brother or sister behind their back? When you sing a song about unity or take Communion, hand that matter over to the Lord. Afterward, if the person you need to talk with privately is there, set up a quiet time to meet instead of rushing to say it on the spot.

lessons.title: Gain Back Your Brother
lessons.hear:
Matthew 18 is often called “the church-life chapter.” Here Jesus gives concrete teaching on what to do when one member of the body sins against another. He lays out a clear path: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother” (Matthew 18:15).

The path has three steps. Step one: go privately—just you and him. Not in the group chat, not in a team meeting, and not by first finding others to take your side. Step two: if he won’t listen, take one or two others along—not to build up a show of force, but to bring mature, fair-minded people who can listen and bear witness together, so that the facts are clear and both sides are protected. Step three: if he still won’t listen, tell the church, and let the church deal with it before the Lord. With each step the circle widens only a little; and each step gives the other person another chance to turn back.

The goal of the whole passage is written right into the first step: “you have gained back your brother.” Not proving I’m right, not making him lose face, but winning a brother back. Strikingly, the passage that comes just before this one is the parable of the lost sheep: the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to go after the one (see Matthew 18:12-14). The path to reconciliation is the heart of the seeking shepherd turned into steps.

Jesus goes on to promise, “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them” (Matthew 18:20). In context, this promise speaks precisely of the hard moments of dealing with a brother’s sin: the Lord himself is present. You are not facing a difficult conversation alone; the Lord goes with you.

One more thing must be made clear. This path is meant for ordinary offenses between members of the body. Where abuse of power, violence, sexual harassment, or other illegal conduct is involved, “go and talk privately first” does not apply. In those cases the first priority is to protect the victim and to seek help from trustworthy leaders, the church’s oversight body, or professional and legal resources.
lessons.light: The self-centered person handles conflict in order to win; the selfless person handles conflict in order to gain someone back. People matter more than issues, and relationships more than winning or losing. That doesn’t mean right and wrong are unimportant—it means right and wrong must serve the goal of gaining the person. To let Jesus reign is to follow his path, not my emotions.
think: In the three steps of Matthew 18:15-17, how does the circle widen at each step?
When I’m wronged, is my heart more set on “winning” or on “gaining back my brother”?
If there is a matter I need to raise privately, how will I prepare my own heart?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the good shepherd who seeks the lost sheep. Put your heart within me, so that when I face someone who has wronged me, I don’t want to win—I only want to gain him back. Give me wisdom too, to discern which matters to raise privately and gently, and which call for seeking help and protection. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write in your journal today: Has someone recently wronged me whom I haven’t gone to directly, but have already talked about with others? If so, confess your talebearing to the Lord and ask him to prepare an opportunity for a private conversation.
lessons.quick: The path to reconciliation has only one goal: to gain back your brother.
text: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.
But if he doesn’t listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.
If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly. If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.
Most certainly I tell you, whatever things you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever things you release on earth will have been released in heaven.
Again, assuredly I tell you, that if two of you will agree on earth concerning anything that they will ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.
For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.”

lessons.title: Restore with Gentleness
lessons.hear:
A sister who had served in children’s ministry for years noticed that her teaching partner was often late, rarely prepared the lessons, and left the children in chaos. She held it in for two months. Then one day she posted a long message in the team group chat listing seven problems. That night her partner left the group chat and never came back to serve. Afterward the sister was heartbroken: “But everything I said was true!” Yes, it was all true—but the place was wrong, the manner was wrong, and her heart had drifted too.

Our old mindset often says, “I’m telling the truth, so I’m not in the wrong.” Or the opposite: “For the sake of peace, don’t say anything.” The first wounds people with the truth; the second excuses sin in the name of peace. Paul offers a third way: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted” (Galatians 6:1).

In the original language, the word “restore” is also used for mending fishing nets and for setting a dislocated bone. A bonesetter’s hands must be both precise and gentle: too much force causes further injury, but doing nothing lets the bone heal crooked. This is exactly the first step of Matthew 18: privately, gently, specifically, and with a heart set on mending.

Paul also says, “looking to yourself.” The person who goes to correct someone else easily falls into a trap—feeling more spiritual than the other. So before you go, look in the mirror: I could fall too; I also stand only by grace. When you go with that humility, the other person won’t feel judged, but will feel the outstretched hand of a companion.

If that sister had quietly invited her partner out for tea and said, “You’ve seemed really busy lately—are you okay? Is there anything I can take off your plate?” perhaps the story would have turned out completely differently.
lessons.light: Humility is returning to my proper place: I am not the judge, just a fellow member of the body who needs grace as much as anyone. The self-centered person uses truth to prove himself right; the selfless person uses truth to restore a brother. Speaking the truth and being gentle are not at odds; both are fruit of the Spirit, both are the life of Christ.
think: In Galatians 6:1-5, what cautions does Paul give to those who go to restore someone?
Am I more prone to wound people with the truth, or to excuse wrongs in the name of peace?
The next time I need to correct someone, how will I “look in the mirror” first?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, forgive me for the times I have wounded people with true words, and for the times I have kept silent out of fear of conflict. Give me a gentle heart and the hands of a bonesetter. Before I go to restore a brother, remind me that I too stand only by grace. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If there is something you need to talk about privately, write down your opening sentence today, in a tone of care rather than accusation—for example: “How have you been lately? There’s something I’d like to talk with you about, just the two of us.”
lessons.quick: Restore a brother with a bonesetter’s hands: precise, yet gentle.
text: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.
But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.
For each man will bear his own burden.

lessons.title: Talk It Over Between You Two
lessons.hear:
Long before Jesus, the Old Testament wisdom books taught the same principle: “Debate your case with your neighbor, and don’t betray the confidence of another” (Proverbs 25:9). In Chinese churches, where relationships and face matter so much, it is all too easy to “tell someone else first.” Often it isn’t that we don’t talk about it—we just talk to the wrong people. We talk to our spouse, to a close friend, to others in the small group—to everyone except the person involved. We say it ten times, the problem isn’t solved even once, and meanwhile the other person’s reputation has already been marked down in five people’s minds.

Today’s practice is learning to talk privately. Here are a few concrete reminders.
1. Timing: Not right after the service when people are coming and going, and not in a long text message. Arrange a quiet time when neither of you is in a hurry—ideally face to face or on the phone.
2. Tone: Start with “I,” not “You always.” “When you said that at the meeting the other day, I felt really hurt” is far easier to hear than “You never respect anyone.”
3. Listening: Once you have said your part, stop and listen. There may be another side of the story you don’t know. James says, “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19).
4. Closing: However it turns out, pray together—or at least say that you value the relationship.

Proverbs says, “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver” (Proverbs 25:11). A fitting word isn’t only right in content; its timing, setting, tone, and heart are right too. Words like that make people willing to turn back.

Remember, too, that a private conversation assumes both people stand on roughly equal and safe footing. If you feel afraid, or if the other person holds authority over you and has abused it before, don’t go alone; talk it over first with someone you trust.
lessons.light: This is where 920 is put into practice: everyone I have a relationship with is one of my “2”—including the one who wronged me. Protecting his reputation is protecting the body of Christ. When I talk with my heart, relying on the Holy Spirit, I am not driven by my emotions; when I talk with my head, relying on myself, the conversation easily turns into a debate contest.
think: What wisdom does Proverbs 25:8-12 give for handling disputes?
Do I often tell others first, without ever talking to the person involved?
If I need to talk privately, what time, place, and opening words will I choose?
lessons.speak: Lord, rule over my mouth, and keep me from telling my brother’s faults to people who have nothing to do with it. Give me courage to speak directly, privately, and gently, and give me a heart willing to listen. May the words I speak be fitting and full of grace, bringing benefit to those who hear. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Concerning the matter that needs attention, take the initiative today to arrange a quiet fifteen-minute conversation this week, in person or by phone. Until it is arranged, don’t mention the matter to any third party.
lessons.quick: Tell the person, not other people; a fitting word is like apples of gold.
text: Don’t be hasty in bringing charges to court. What will you do in the end when your neighbor shames you?
Debate your case with your neighbor, and don’t betray the confidence of another,
lest one who hears it put you to shame, and your bad reputation never depart.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.
As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover to an obedient ear.

lessons.title: This Path Is Not for Silencing
lessons.hear:
Any good tool can be misused, and the Matthew 18 path to reconciliation is no exception. In some places victims have been told, “The Bible says to go privately first—how could you tell anyone else?” And so the oppressed are sent back to face the very person who oppressed them, or even told to keep quiet “for the sake of unity.” That is a serious misuse of the Lord’s word.

The Old Testament contains a heartbreaking account. David’s daughter Tamar was violated by her half-brother Amnon. Yet her full brother Absalom said to her, “But now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother. Don’t take this thing to heart” (2 Samuel 13:20). When King David heard of it, “he was very angry” (2 Samuel 13:21)—yet he did nothing. As a result, Tamar “remained desolate,” while hatred quietly festered in the family and later erupted into an even greater tragedy. Demanding silence because “he is your brother” has never been reconciliation; it only wounds the wounded person all over again.

So we must draw a clear distinction. Matthew 18:15 speaks of ordinary offenses between members of the body—a hurtful word, a broken promise, a misunderstanding. Where abuse of power, violence, sexual harassment or assault, financial misconduct, or other illegal acts are involved, “talk privately first” does not apply. Instead we should first protect the victim’s safety; seek help from a trustworthy pastor, the church’s oversight body, or professionals; and, when necessary, call the police and pursue the matter through legal channels. God’s word says, “Open your mouth for the mute, in the cause of all who are left desolate” (Proverbs 31:8).

Today, review your own heart honestly as well. Have I ever used “unity” or “forgiveness” to suppress the voice of someone who was hurt? Have I ever skipped the private conversation and gone straight to talking about someone behind their back? These two errors point in opposite directions, and both need adjusting: in the first case, I must learn to stand beside the one who suffers; in the second, I must learn to go to the person directly.
lessons.light: Pride is grasping power that does not belong to us. Abuse of power is exactly that—and so is silencing people to protect our reputation. A humble church is willing to lay down the power to protect its own name and return to its proper place of protecting the weak. In a church where Jesus reigns, light matters more than face, and victims matter more than image.
think: In 2 Samuel 13:19-22, what were the results of Absalom’s and David’s responses?
Have I ever used “unity” or “forgiveness” to demand silence from someone who was hurt?
If someone tells me they are being mistreated, how should my first response and help look?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the righteous God and a refuge for the oppressed. Forgive us for the times we have demanded silence from the hurting to save face, and forgive me for skipping the private conversation and talking about people behind their backs. Make our church a safe place that dares to speak up for those who have no voice, and that also goes gently to a brother who has done wrong. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Spend ten minutes today finding out what channels for help your church or denomination has if someone in the church is being mistreated or abused. Write down one trustworthy contact so that you can help someone if the need arises.
lessons.quick: For ordinary offenses, talk privately first; for abuse and harm, protect the victim and seek help first.
text: Tamar put ashes on her head, and tore her garment of various colors that was on her; and she laid her hand on her head and went her way, crying aloud as she went.

Absalom her brother said to her, “Has Amnon your brother been with you? But now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother. Don’t take this thing to heart.” So Tamar remained desolate in her brother Absalom’s house.
But when King David heard of all these things, he was very angry.
Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad; for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had forced his sister Tamar.

lessons.title: Turning Back the Wanderer
lessons.hear:
This week we have walked a path: go and speak privately, bring one or two others along, tell the church. It looks like a procedure, but it is really a heart. James ends his letter this way: “Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back, let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:19-20).

Notice that James doesn’t say “if the elders of the church turn him back,” but “someone.” This isn’t work reserved for pastors; it is something every member of the body can take part in. One brother, looking back on the years he spent away from church, said, “Nobody came to scold me—but nobody came looking for me either. Then a friend from my old small group started sending me a message once a month, and he didn’t miss a month for three years. I came back because of him.”

For this path to reconciliation to take root in the church, it has to be passed on from one generation to the next. If you are a small group leader, you can read Matthew 18:15-17 together with your group and discuss: “When we sin against one another, how do we want to handle it?” When everyone agrees ahead of time, there is less panic when conflict comes. If you are a parent, you can teach your children: “If someone upsets you, go and talk to them first—don’t tell the whole class first.” That is how we plant God’s culture in the hearts of the next generation.

Pass on the boundaries we learned this week as well: for ordinary offenses, go and speak privately first; for abuse and harm, protect first and seek help first. Truth and grace, gentleness and justice, never cancel each other out in the body of the Lord.
lessons.light: The last of the eight steps of changing a mindset is multiplication. The 235 relationships of spiritual companions are the best soil for this path to reconciliation: when we have companions, there is someone willing to tell us the truth privately; when we have spiritual parents, there is someone to gently pull us back when we drift.
think: According to James 5:19-20, what does the one who turns someone back accomplish?
What new insight have I gained this week about “showing a brother his fault”?
With whom can I share this path to reconciliation, or how can I bring it into my small group?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you that you didn’t give up on me when I wandered, and that you sent someone to bring me back. Make me the “someone” your word speaks of, who doesn’t give up on brothers and sisters drifting away. Help me pass on your path to reconciliation—your heart of gentleness and justice—to my small group and to the next generation. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a brother or sister who hasn’t been to church for some time, and send them a greeting today with no hint of blame: “It’s been a long time—I miss you, and I’ve been praying for you.” Then plan to reach out again next month.
lessons.quick: The “someone” who turns a brother back can be me.
text: Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back,
let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.

weeks.title: Seventy Times Seven and the Witness of Unity
weeks.keyText: being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
weeks.theme: Forgiveness breaks the chains of bitterness; a church that forgives one another lets the world recognize Jesus.
group: Read Matthew 18:21-35. Where did the servant who was forgiven ten thousand talents go wrong?
Without naming the other person, can you share whether there is a debt in your heart that you just can’t let go of?
How can we practice “being eager to keep the unity” together this week, and what one action will we choose to do for one another?
weeks.sunday: “Being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3). Before the service, bring to the Lord a debt in your heart that you can’t let go of. During the service, look at the brothers and sisters around you from different backgrounds and give thanks for your unity. Afterward, make a point of sitting with or greeting someone you rarely talk to.

lessons.title: Not Seven, but Seventy Times Seven
lessons.hear:
Peter probably thought he was being very generous. If the same person sinned against him seven times and he still forgave, that was already far more than most people could put up with. So he asked Jesus, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?” (Matthew 18:21). Jesus’ answer left him speechless: “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22).

Jesus doesn’t mean that we should count to four hundred ninety and then take revenge on the four hundred ninety-first time. He means that forgiveness is not a matter of counting. As long as you are still counting, your heart is still keeping the books.

Then Jesus told a parable. A servant owed the king ten thousand talents—a sum an ordinary laborer could not repay in thousands of lifetimes. The king, “being moved with compassion, released him, and forgave him the debt” (Matthew 18:27). But as soon as that servant went out, he found a fellow servant who owed him a hundred denarii, “and he grabbed him, and took him by the throat” (Matthew 18:28). The gap between the two debts is absurdly large.

The key to the parable lies in the king’s question: “Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?” (Matthew 18:33). The strength to forgive doesn’t come from gritting our teeth; it comes from remembering how much we ourselves have been forgiven. When I see the price the Lord paid for me on the cross, what others owe me—real and painful as it is—can never be bigger than grace.

Let’s also be clear: forgiveness does not mean pretending it never happened. It doesn’t mean the harm wasn’t serious, and it doesn’t mean trust is restored right away. Forgiveness means handing back to God my right to judge and to collect the debt, and no longer letting bitterness reign in my heart. The Lord wants us to forgive “from your hearts” (Matthew 18:35). That is often a process. It takes time, it takes tears, and it takes people walking with us—but it can begin today, with “I am willing.”
lessons.light: Refusing to forgive is sitting on the judgment throne that belongs to God alone; forgiving is returning to my proper place as a sinner who has received grace, and letting God be God. Bitterness is like drinking poison yourself and waiting for the other person to fall down. The selfless life hands the ledger over to the Lord, and the heart is set free.
think: In Matthew 18:21-35, how different are the two debts, and what does the king say at the end?
Am I still keeping a ledger in my heart of what others owe me?
Which debt am I willing to begin handing over to the Lord today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, the debt you have forgiven me is one I could never repay in my whole life. Forgive me for clinging so tightly to the hundred denarii others owe me. I may not be able to let go of all the pain at once, but today I am willing to begin handing my right to judge back to you. Heal my wounds and help me forgive from my heart. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today write down a person or situation you find very hard to forgive (for the Lord’s eyes only). Beside it write: “Lord, you forgave me ten thousand talents; I am willing to begin handing this debt over to you.” If you can’t do that yet, first ask the Lord to make you willing.
lessons.quick: As long as you’re counting, you’re keeping the books; remember grace, and you can begin to forgive.
text: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?”
Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.
Therefore the Kingdom of Heaven is like a certain king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants.
When he had begun to settle, one was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents.
But because he couldn’t pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, with his wife, his children, and all that he had, and payment to be made.
The servant therefore fell down and knelt before him, saying, ‘Lord, have patience with me, and I will repay you all!’
The lord of that servant, being moved with compassion, released him and forgave him the debt.
“But that servant went out and found one of his fellow servants who owed him one hundred denarii, and he grabbed him and took him by the throat, saying, ‘Pay me what you owe!’
“So his fellow servant fell down at his feet and begged him, saying, ‘Have patience with me, and I will repay you!’
He would not, but went and cast him into prison until he should pay back that which was due.
So when his fellow servants saw what was done, they were exceedingly sorry, and came and told their lord all that was done.
Then his lord called him in and said to him, ‘You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you begged me.
Shouldn’t you also have had mercy on your fellow servant, even as I had mercy on you?’
His lord was angry, and delivered him to the tormentors until he should pay all that was due to him.
So my heavenly Father will also do to you, if you don’t each forgive your brother from your hearts for his misdeeds.”

lessons.title: Am I in the Place of God?
lessons.hear:
A sister in a small group had, years earlier, been slandered behind her back by a co-worker she trusted deeply, and as a result she stepped down from her place of service. She said, “It’s not that I don’t want to forgive. I just feel that if I forgive him, it’s like saying he did nothing wrong—and then what was all my suffering for?” Many people feel exactly the same. Our old mindset assumes: forgiving = acting as if nothing happened = letting the person who hurt me get away with it.

Joseph’s story gives us God’s perspective. Joseph was sold into Egypt by his brothers and suffered one injustice after another. Years later he became the ruler of Egypt. When their father Jacob died, his brothers were afraid he would take revenge. When Joseph heard their plea, he wept and said, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?” (Genesis 50:19).

That sentence is the heart of forgiveness. Joseph did not say, “You did nothing wrong.” He said plainly, “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive” (Genesis 50:20). He acknowledged that evil was evil and the harm was real; but he no longer stood in God’s place to judge and to take revenge. He saw a bigger picture: God was still sovereign over human evil, and could make all things work together for good.

Notice, too, that Joseph’s road to this point was not short. He once tested his brothers to see whether they had really changed (see Genesis 42:14-17), and he wept more than once. Forgiveness and rebuilding trust are two different things: forgiveness can be a one-sided decision, but trust requires genuine change on the other side, and it takes time.

That sister later said the biggest change wasn’t that the other person came to apologize—he never did. It was that she finally stopped replaying what had happened in her mind every day. She handed judgment over to God and found freedom for herself. The first person forgiveness sets free is the one who forgives.
lessons.light: “Am I in the place of God?” This is the very definition of humility: laying down power, returning to my proper place, and letting God be God. The self-centered person wants to get justice with his own hands; the selfless person entrusts justice to the God who is just. From a human point of view there is only harm; from God’s point of view, even harm can be turned into blessing.
think: In Genesis 50:15-21, how does Joseph both acknowledge his brothers’ evil and refuse to take revenge?
Do I think that “forgiving” means “acting as if nothing happened”?
What hurt do I need to learn to see again from God’s perspective?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I often want to take your place and get justice with my own hands. Today I acknowledge that judgment belongs to you, not to me. Let me see that you are still sovereign in my pain, and give me strength to let go of the desire for revenge. Even if the other person never apologizes, may I find freedom in you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today reread Genesis 50:19-20 and rewrite Joseph’s words as your own prayer: “He meant evil against me, but God meant…” Write down the good you believe God can bring out of it.
lessons.quick: Forgiveness doesn’t say he did nothing wrong; it says, “I am not in the place of God.”
text: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.”
They sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father commanded before he died, saying,

‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.”
Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.
Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.

lessons.title: Just as God Forgave You
lessons.hear:
Forgiveness is not only a feeling; it is also a series of choices we can practice. Paul says, “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice. And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:31-32).

Notice the order of this list: bitterness comes first. Bitterness is the root; wrath and anger are the stem; outcry and slander are the fruit. If we deal only with the quarrels on the surface and don’t pull up the bitterness in our hearts, it will grow back before long.

Today, try doing three concrete things.
1. Say it. Tell the Lord specifically what happened and how much it hurt. Don’t brush it off with “Oh, forget it.” God wants to heal real wounds, not a version of you that pretends it doesn’t hurt.
2. Hand it over. Declare to the Lord in one sentence: “Lord, what he owes me, I hand over to you.” When the scene replays in your mind again, say it again. Forgiveness often has to be repeated many times; that is another layer of meaning in “seventy times seven.”
3. Speak well. “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be” (Ephesians 4:29). Stop bringing the matter up in front of others today, and if you have the chance, say something good about the other person that is true.

If the harm is still going on, or involves mistreatment or violence, forgiveness does not require you to return to danger. You can forgive while keeping a safe distance, and seek the support and help of people you trust. Forgiveness hands revenge over to God; it does not hand you over to harm.
lessons.light: “Just as God also in Christ forgave you”—the measure of forgiveness isn’t whether the other person deserves it, but how much grace I have received. When I live from the heart, relying on the Holy Spirit, I am not dragged along by the replays of the past; when I live from the head, relying on myself, I keep settling accounts over and over. Pulling up the root of bitterness is letting Jesus reign over my emotions.
think: What does Ephesians 4:29-32 tell us to put away, and what does it tell us to live out?
Which event keeps “replaying” in my heart?
How will I concretely say it, hand it over, and speak well today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, on the cross you asked the Father to forgive those who crucified you. Put that same heart within me. Today I tell you specifically what happened, and I hand it over to you. When it surfaces again, Holy Spirit, remind me to hand it over again, and help me stop speaking bitter words. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Practice “handing it over” today: whenever the matter surfaces in your mind, stop and say, “Lord, what he owes me, I hand over to you.” Before bed, note how many times you handed it over today, and thank the Lord for your progress.
lessons.quick: Say it, hand it over, speak well: pull up the root of bitterness.
text: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.
Don’t grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.
Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice.
And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.

lessons.title: Euodia and Syntyche
lessons.hear:
Philippians is Paul’s warmest letter, overflowing with joy from beginning to end. But in chapter 4 he suddenly names two sisters: “I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord” (Philippians 4:2). These two were not people on the fringe; “they labored with me in the Good News” (Philippians 4:3)—they were core co-workers in the church. We don’t know why they quarreled. Perhaps they simply had different ways of serving. But it had become serious enough that Paul brought it up in a letter the whole church would hear.

This is a mirror for us. The hardest conflicts in a church are often not between strangers but between co-workers who have labored side by side for years. The more invested we are, the stronger our opinions; and the stronger our opinions, the easier it is to feel that “my way is the right way.”

Paul’s way of handling it is worth learning from. First, he doesn’t take sides; he uses the same word, “exhort,” for both women. Second, he isn’t asking them to agree on everything, but to think the same way in the Lord—their methods may differ, but their hearts must be aligned with the same Lord. Third, he asks his “true partner” to “help these women” (Philippians 4:3). Unity isn’t only the business of the two people involved; it also needs someone alongside who will gently accompany and help.

Today, review your heart before the Lord: Am I a Euodia or a Syntyche? Is there a co-worker with whom I am outwardly polite, but with whom my heart has long since parted ways? On the other hand, have I ever taken sides in a conflict between two brothers or sisters, carried messages, or added fuel to the fire? Or am I willing to be that true partner who helps both sides come back before the Lord?

The first step of adjustment might simply be a phone call: “I feel like we’ve gotten a bit stuck. Could we pray together?”
lessons.light: Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Disunity among co-workers is often a case of “my way” wanting to reign. To let Jesus reign is to lay “my way is right” at his feet—to be of one mind in the Lord, not merely to agree on the task.
think: In Philippians 4:1-3, how does Paul handle the disagreement between two co-workers?
With which co-worker or church member am I outwardly polite but no longer of one heart?
How can I become a “true partner” who helps others be reconciled?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that in ministry I often value my own methods more than my co-workers’ hearts. Search me, and wherever there is disunity, give me courage to be the first to mend it. Keep me from carrying messages or taking sides in other people’s conflicts; make me someone who helps both sides come back to you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: If there is distance between you and a co-worker, invite them today to pray together for ten minutes this week. If you know of two brothers or sisters who are at odds, pray for each of them today, and ask the Lord to show you whether you should step in to help.
lessons.quick: We don’t have to agree on everything, but we must be of one mind in the Lord.
text: Therefore, my brothers, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, my beloved.
I exhort Euodia, and I exhort Syntyche, to think the same way in the Lord.
Yes, I beg you also, true partner, help these women, for they labored with me in the Good News with Clement also, and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.

lessons.title: That the World May Believe
lessons.hear:
On the night he was betrayed, Jesus prayed for his disciples—and for everyone in every generation who would believe in him. That means that on that night the Lord prayed for you and your church too. What did he ask for? “That they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me” (John 17:21).

The unity of the church isn’t only about making us comfortable with one another; it is a witness. When the world looks at the church, people rarely read our statement of faith first. They first watch how we treat each other. When two brothers who once hurt each other embrace at the Lord’s Table, when a church that has been through a split is willing to confess its sins to one another and start over, the world asks, “What power is this?” Jesus said, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

Unity is not uniformity. An orchestra needs different instruments; a family needs different personalities. Unity is sharing one life and facing one Lord in the midst of diversity. That is why Paul urges us to be “eager to keep the unity of the Spirit” (Ephesians 4:3). Unity is given by the Holy Spirit; we don’t manufacture it. But we must be eager to keep it, like shielding a lamp so the wind doesn’t blow it out. And the tool we use most often to keep unity is the very thing we have learned this week: forgiveness. The psalmist marveled long ago: “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1).

If you have moved forward even a little on the road of forgiveness this week—even just one small step—please tell a brother or sister about it. Your testimony may be where someone else begins to put down their ledger. That is how unity spreads: one person at a time.
lessons.light: One purpose of the 321 Vision is to build God’s system, so that God’s kingdom comes and his will is done on earth. The unity of the church is heaven’s pattern made visible on earth. The “0” in 920 stands for selflessness, and only selfless people can truly be one. When each of us no longer wants to reign, Jesus reigns among us.
think: In John 17:20-23, what is the purpose of Jesus’ prayer for unity?
What have I experienced this week in forgiveness and unity?
With whom will I share this experience, and how will I encourage them to keep unity?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for praying for me on that night too. May our church be one, so that the world may believe in you. Holy Spirit, help me be eager to keep the unity—to mend cracks with forgiveness and to bind us together with love—so that people recognize you in the way we treat one another. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Sometime this week, share with your spiritual companion or small group one small step you have taken toward forgiveness (no need to name the other person), then pray together for five minutes for the unity of the church.
lessons.quick: Forgiveness keeps unity, and unity lets the world recognize Jesus.
text: “Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word,
that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.
The glory which you have given me, I have given to them, that they may be one, even as we are one,
I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, that the world may know that you sent me and loved them, even as you loved me.
